From equation (17.18), \(x(-1) = x_1 = 0\) and \(x(1) = x_3 = L\), because \(N_1(-1) = 1\) and \(N_3(1) = 1\) and the other two functions vanish at these points. By the lemma on the inverse function (lemma 8.9) \(x\) is a bijection onto \([0, L]\), and its inverse is differentiable at interior points with derivative \(1/x'(\xi) = 1/J\). In figure 17.39 these are the curves of the middle panel, which rise everywhere from \(0\) to \(1\): every height \(x/L\) belongs to exactly one \(\xi\).
  2. By the chain rule (lemma 4.43), \(u_{\mathrm{h}}'(x) = U'(\xi(x))\,\xi'(x) = U'(\xi)/J(\xi)\). The change of the field per unit of \(\xi\) is spread over \(J\) units of length of the bar.
  3. Let \(G\) be a primitive function of \(g\), which exists by theorem 3.55. By the chain rule \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\xi}\,G(x(\xi)) = g(x(\xi))\,J(\xi)\), and by the same theorem \(\int_{-1}^{1} g(x(\xi))\,J\,\mathrm{d}\xi = G(x(1)) - G(x(-1)) = G(L) - G(0) = \int_0^L g\,\mathrm{d}x\). In the figure these are the equal areas.
  4. By point 2, \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}' = N_{\mathrm{i}}'/J\). We insert it into \(\int_0^L EA\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\) and use point 3 with \(g = EA\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\): we get \(EA \int (N_{\mathrm{i}}'/J)(N_{\mathrm{j}}'/J)\,J\,\mathrm{d}\xi\), which is the claim.

Source: COOK, section 6.1, PDF pp. 218 to 219: the strain \((\mathrm{d}u/\mathrm{d}\xi)/J\) and the stiffness matrix with \(J\) in the denominator, which cannot easily be integrated in closed form, so it is computed by Gauss integration. The proof in steps is ours.

If \(c = \tfrac12\), then \(J = L/2\) is constant and the integrand in point 4 is a polynomial, as in section 7.4. For other \(c\) the \(J\) is in the denominator, the integrand is a rational function and the Gauss rule (definition 7.24) is no longer exact: the rule with \(q\) points gives the true integral for polynomials up to degree \(2q - 1\), and a fraction with \(J\) in the denominator is not a polynomial of any degree. The lemma therefore owes us a statement of when \(J > 0\) holds at all.

17.5.2 Where the middle node may be

The condition \(J > 0\) is a condition on \(c\). Since \(J\) is a straight line in \(\xi\), its two end values, which the figure shows at the edges of the right panel, are all we need to know.

Figure 17.41 shows why the end values suffice. The line \(J\) runs along the axis \(\xi\) over \([-1, 1]\) from \(J(-1)\) at the left end to \(J(1)\) at the right. At a chosen point \(\xi\) the base is split into two pieces: the right one, of length \(1 - \xi\), and the left one, of length \(1 + \xi\). Their shares of the whole length \(2\) are the weights of the end values, and the height of the line above the point is their sum.

Lemma 17.22 Admissible position of the middle node (dovoljena lega srednjega vozlišča)

Let a bar element have the nodes \(0\), \(c\,L\) and \(L\) with \(0 < c < 1\).

  1. \(J(-1) = L\,(2c - \tfrac12)\) and \(J(1) = L\,(\tfrac32 - 2c)\).
  2. \(J(\xi) > 0\) for every \(\xi \in [-1, 1]\) if and only if \(\tfrac14 < c < \tfrac34\).
  3. If \(c \le \tfrac14\) or \(c \ge \tfrac34\), then \(J\) has a zero \(\xi_0 = 1/(2(2c - 1))\) in \([-1, 1]\). For \(c < \tfrac14\) we have \(x(\xi_0) = L\,\big(c - 1/(8(1 - 2c))\big) < 0\) and \(x\) is not monotone: the same point of the bar has two values of \(\xi\) and the element sticks out over node 1.
Proof

We must show the end values of \(J\), that the positivity of a straight line is positivity at both ends, and find the zero.

  1. We insert \(\xi = \mp 1\) into equation (17.19): \(J(-1) = L(\tfrac12 - 1 + 2c)\) and \(J(1) = L(\tfrac12 + 1 - 2c)\).
  2. By equation (17.19) the function \(J\) is linear in \(\xi\), so each of its values on \([-1, 1]\) lies between \(J(-1)\) and \(J(1)\): for every \(\xi\) we have \(J(\xi) = \tfrac{1 - \xi}{2}\,J(-1) + \tfrac{1 + \xi}{2}\,J(1)\) (inserting point 1 gives equation (17.19)) with nonnegative weights whose sum is \(1\). If both end values are positive, every value is positive. Conversely, positivity at the ends is necessary. Point 1 turns \(J(-1) > 0\) into \(c > \tfrac14\) and \(J(1) > 0\) into \(c < \tfrac34\). In figure 17.39 these are the left ends of the lines: at \(c = 0{,}4\) and \(0{,}3\) they are above the axis, at \(c = 0{,}25\) it is on the axis.
  3. From \(J(\xi_0) = 0\) and equation (17.19) we have \((1 - 2c)\,\xi_0 = -\tfrac12\), so \(\xi_0 = 1/(2(2c - 1))\). The condition \(|\xi_0| \le 1\) is \(|2c - 1| \ge \tfrac12\), that is \(c \le \tfrac14\) or \(c \ge \tfrac34\). For \(c < \tfrac14\) we have \(J(-1) < 0 < J(1)\), so \(x'\) changes sign at \(\xi_0\), where \(x\) has its smallest value. Inserting \(\xi_0\) into equation (17.18) gives \(x(\xi_0) = L\,(c - \tfrac{1}{4(1 - 2c)} + \tfrac{1}{8(1 - 2c)}) = L\,(c - \tfrac{1}{8(1 - 2c)})\). In figure 17.39 this is the grey curve for \(c = 0{,}1\): \(J/L\) goes from \(-0{,}3\) to \(1{,}3\) and crosses the axis at \(\xi_0 = -0{,}625\), and the map descends there to \(x = -0{,}056\,L\) below the axis and returns to \(0\) at \(\xi = -0{,}25\). The piece between \(-0{,}056\,L\) and \(0\) is therefore covered twice.

Source: The proof is not from the source. COOK, PDF p. 250: "An acceptably shaped element should not display negative J at any Gauss point location."

The proof showed that the positivity of \(J\) is a question of two numbers and that at a quarter and three quarters of the length we are at the edge. This is the grey band on the left panel of the figure: the nodes \(c = 0{,}4\) and \(c = 0{,}3\) are inside it, the node \(c = 0{,}25\) is on its edge. Now a test that at the same time shows that the condition \(J > 0\) is not yet sufficient.

Example 17.23 Middle node off the centre, field \(u = x^2\) (premaknjeno vozlišče pri polju \(u = x^2\))

Take \(L = 1\) and the displacement \(u = x^2\) with the strain \(2x\), which grows from \(0\) to \(2\). The nodal values are \(d = (0, c^2, 1)\), and the element equals \(u\) everywhere where \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = x^2\). At \(c = \tfrac12\) the function \(x(\xi)\) is linear, so \(x(\xi)^2\) is a polynomial of degree two in \(\xi\), which \(N_1, N_2, N_3\) represent exactly (they have the same values in the nodes): \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = x^2\) and the strain is exact, the error is \(0\).

At \(c \ne \tfrac12\) the coefficient of \(\xi^4\) in \(x(\xi)^2\) is \((2c - 1)^2/4 \ne 0\) (SymPy), while the field \(U(\xi)\) has degree at most \(2\). Polynomials of degree \(4\) and \(2\) do not agree everywhere, so \(u_{\mathrm{h}} \ne x^2\). The largest strain error is at the left end, where the true \(2x = 0\). There \(U'(-1) = 2d_2 - d_3/2 = 2c^2 - \tfrac12\) and \(J(-1) = 2c - \tfrac12\), so by point 2 of lemma 17.21

\[u_{\mathrm{h}}'(0) = \frac{2c^2 - \frac12}{2c - \frac12} . \tag{17.20}\]

The numbers, computed with SymPy and NumPy, are:

\(c\) \(J(-1)/L\) largest strain error \(k_{11}\,L/EA\) exact with 2 points with 3 points
\(0{,}5\) \(0{,}50\) \(0\) \(2{,}3333\) \(2{,}3333\) \(2{,}3333\)
\(0{,}4\) \(0{,}30\) \(0{,}60\) \(3{,}1284\) \(3{,}0282\) \(3{,}1239\)
\(0{,}3\) \(0{,}10\) \(3{,}20\) \(5{,}5725\) \(4{,}3220\) \(5{,}2424\)
\(0{,}26\) \(0{,}02\) \(18{,}24\) \(10{,}7635\) \(5{,}2156\) \(7{,}5330\)

At \(c = 0{,}26\) we have \(J > 0\) by lemma 17.22, so the element is admissible, but the strain error is \(9\) times the largest true strain \(2\). Figure 17.42 shows the cause. On the left panel the strain is drawn above the axis \(x\) of the element. At \(c = 0{,}5\) it coincides with the true straight line \(2x\). For the other fractions the strain of the element oscillates near the left end far from the true straight line, because \(J\) is small in the denominator while \(U'(-1)\) in the numerator is not zero. At \(x = 0\), where the true strain is \(0\), it falls to \(-0{,}6\) at \(c = 0{,}4\) and to \(-3{,}2\) at \(c = 0{,}3\), which are the errors \(0{,}60\) and \(3{,}20\) of the table. The curve for \(c = 0{,}26\) would reach \(-18{,}24\), five times below the bottom edge of the figure, so it is not drawn. The stiffness entry \(k_{11}\) is also computed ever worse: at \(c = 0{,}3\) the two-point rule misses by \(22\,\%\) and three points by \(6\,\%\), because the rational integrand with a small denominator rises sharply at the end (definition 7.24).

Positivity of \(J\) is thus a necessary condition for the element to exist, but not a sufficient condition for its quality. The measure of quality is how little \(J\) changes over the element: at \(c = 0{,}5\) not at all, at \(c = 0{,}26\) by a factor of \(49\), from \(J(-1)/L = 0{,}02\) to \(J(1)/L = 0{,}98\). Below the limit, at \(c = 0{,}2\) (as for the grey curve at \(c = 0{,}1\)), we have \(J(-1)/L = -0{,}10\), \(\xi_0 = -0{,}8333\) and \(x(\xi_0) = -0{,}00833\,L\) (lemma 17.22, point 3). So the element sticks out \(0{,}83\,\%\) of its length beyond the end of the bar. The strain has a pole inside, because at \(\xi_0\) the denominator \(J\) is zero while the numerator is not: for the nodal values of the field \(u = x^2\) of the example, \(U'(\xi_0) = -0{,}27\). A check of the sign of \(J\) at the Gauss points only does not always see this. With two points the left point \(\xi = -0{,}577\) has \(J/L = 0{,}15\), with three points the point \(\xi = -0{,}775\) has \(0{,}035\). Both are positive, because both points lie to the right of \(\xi_0\). Since \(J\) is a straight line, the reliable check is the sign at both ends (lemma 17.22, point 2).

17.5.3 The quarter-point (četrtinska točka)

We marked the limit \(c = \tfrac14\) as inadmissible, yet programs use it there on purpose. Figure 17.42 shows why: on the right panel the error of the field \(u_{\mathrm{h}} - \sqrt{x}\) at \(c = 0{,}25\) is exactly zero, while for other fractions it is in size up to \(0{,}14\) (at \(c = 0{,}5\), near \(x = 0{,}09\)). An element with a quarter point represents the square root exactly. Why is the square root interesting? Because in a linearly elastic body with a crack the stress near the crack tip behaves like \(1/\sqrt r\), where \(r\) is the distance from the tip (COOK, section 8.7, PDF p. 298). If the strain is proportional to \(r^{-1/2}\), the displacement is by the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.55) proportional to \(2\sqrt r\). Ordinary elements cannot represent such a strain (ibid.). It turns out that an element with a moved node can.

Figure 17.43 shows why the coordinate \(s\) is natural at the quarter point. On the \(x\) axis the nodes are at \(0\), \(L/4\) and \(L\). Below it is the \(s\) axis, on which the same nodes are at \(0\), \(\tfrac12\) and \(1\), evenly spaced, and links show \(s = \sqrt{x/L}\). In \(s\) the shape functions \(N_1\), \(N_2\), \(N_3\) are parabolas that equal \(1\) at their own node and \(0\) at the other two, and the element field is their sum with weights \(d_1\), \(d_2\), \(d_3\).

Corollary 17.24 Quarter-point element (element s četrtinsko točko)

Let \(c = \tfrac14\) and \(s = \sqrt{x/L}\). Then:

  1. The map \(x(\xi) = L\,(1 + \xi)^2/4\), so \(\xi = 2s - 1\), and \(J(\xi) = L\,(1 + \xi)/2\) has a zero at \(\xi = -1\).
  2. The element field with displacements \(d_1, d_2, d_3\) is \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = d_1 + a\,s + b\,s^2\) with \(a = 4d_2 - 3d_1 - d_3\) and \(b = 2\,(d_1 - 2d_2 + d_3)\). For \(x > 0\) we have \(u_{\mathrm{h}}' = \dfrac{a}{2\sqrt{xL}} + \dfrac{b}{L}\).
  3. The field \(u = \sqrt{x/L}\) with displacements \((0, \tfrac12, 1)\) is represented exactly by the element (\(a = 1\), \(b = 0\)), and so are a constant field and the field \(u = x/L\) with displacements \((0, \tfrac14, 1)\) (\(a = 0\), \(b = 1\)).
Proof

We must show the map, the form of the field in \(s\) and three values.

  1. Inserting \(c = \tfrac14\) into equation (17.18) gives \(x = L(\tfrac14 + \tfrac\xi2 + \tfrac{\xi^2}4) = L(1 + \xi)^2/4\) and into equation (17.19) \(J = L(1 + \xi)/2\) (SymPy). In figure 17.39 this is the dashed parabola, which touches the axis at \(\xi = -1\) with a horizontal tangent, and the line \(J\) that reaches zero there. Since \(1 + \xi \ge 0\) on the element, \(s = (1 + \xi)/2\).
  2. At \(\xi = 2s - 1\) we have the shape functions \(N_1 = 2s^2 - 3s + 1\), \(N_2 = 4s - 4s^2\) and \(N_3 = 2s^2 - s\). The sum \(d_1N_1 + d_2N_2 + d_3N_3\) gives \(d_1 + a\,s + b\,s^2\) with the stated \(a\) and \(b\). The derivative follows by the chain rule (lemma 4.43) with \(s' = 1/(2\sqrt{xL})\) and \(b\,(s^2)' = b/L\).
  3. For \(\sqrt{x/L}\) the nodal values are \(0\), \(\sqrt{1/4} = \tfrac12\), \(1\), so \(a = 2 - 1 = 1\) and \(b = 2(0 - 1 + 1) = 0\), which is \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = s\). For \(x/L = s^2\) we have \(d = (0, \tfrac14, 1)\) and \(a = 0\), \(b = 2(-\tfrac12 + 1) = 1\), so \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = s^2\). A constant field \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = d\) gives \(a = b = 0\).

Source: COOK, section 8.7, equation (8.7-3) and the text, PDF pp. 298 to 299: for \(x \ll L\) the strain is inversely proportional to \(\sqrt x\), the element keeps rigid-body motion and constant strain. The proof in steps is ours.

The proof showed that the field \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) contains \(\sqrt{x}\), \(x\) and a constant, and that the strain is unbounded whenever \(a \ne 0\). But unboundedness has a price, which in a book about the bar we must not conceal. Ritz's method (chapter 6) requires fields of finite energy (definition 6.18).

Lemma 17.25 Energy of the quarter-point element in one dimension (energija elementa s četrtinsko točko v eni razsežnosti)

At \(c = \tfrac14\) and \(a \ne 0\) from corollary 17.24, the energy \(\int_\delta^L EA\,(u_{\mathrm{h}}')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) is unbounded as \(\delta \to 0\), namely \(\frac{EA\,a^2}{4L}\ln(L/\delta)\) plus a bounded term. Only the fields with \(a = 0\), that is with \(d_3 = 4d_2 - 3d_1\), have finite energy, and these are the straight lines \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = d_1 + b\,x/L\).

Proof

We must show the expansion of the square of the strain and the integral of each term.

  1. By corollary 17.24, \((u_{\mathrm{h}}')^2 = \dfrac{a^2}{4xL} + \dfrac{ab}{L\sqrt{xL}} + \dfrac{b^2}{L^2}\).
  2. By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.55), \(\int_\delta^L \dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x = \ln\dfrac L\delta\), \(\int_\delta^L x^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}x = 2\,(\sqrt L - \sqrt\delta)\) and \(\int_\delta^L \mathrm{d}x = L - \delta\). The last two integrals are bounded for every \(\delta \in (0, L)\), the first exceeds every bound as \(\delta \to 0\).
  3. So the energy equals \(\frac{EA\,a^2}{4L}\ln\frac L\delta\) plus a bounded part, and it is unbounded if \(a \ne 0\) (the orange straight line, which grows without end). The condition \(a = 0\) is \(d_3 = 4d_2 - 3d_1\), and then \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = d_1 + b\,s^2 = d_1 + b\,x/L\).

Source: The proof is not from the source.

A test with numbers, the field \(u = \sqrt{x}\) (\(L = EA = 1\), \(d = (0, \tfrac12, 1)\), \(a = 1\), \(b = 0\)): the energy on \([\delta, 1]\) is \(1{,}15\), \(2{,}30\), \(3{,}45\) and \(4{,}61\) for \(\delta = 10^{-2}\), \(10^{-4}\), \(10^{-6}\), \(10^{-8}\) (SymPy). Figure 17.44 has on the horizontal axis \(\delta\), which decreases to the right, each mark a hundred times smaller than the one before. Every hundredfold smaller \(\delta\) adds \(1{,}15 = \tfrac14\ln 100\), as the lemma predicts with the factor \(\frac{EA\,a^2}{4L} = \tfrac14\), so the points lie on a straight line that does not stop. The field \(u = x\) (\(d = (0, \tfrac14, 1)\), \(a = 0\)) has the energy \(1 - \delta\), which is less than \(1\) for every \(\delta\).

A program that computes the stiffness with the Gauss rule gets finite numbers, \(k_{11} = 5{,}5\) with two and \(8{,}5\) with three points (SymPy and NumPy). The two numbers differ, and the true value is infinite, because \(k_{11}\) is the energy of the field \(\psi_1\) with \(d = (1, 0, 0)\), which has \(a = -3 \ne 0\). Therefore the quarter point in a bar is a poor element: either it has infinite energy, or it represents only straight lines, which the linear element already does.

For a plane element it is different. Figure 17.45 shows a crack with its tip at the origin. Around the tip lies an annulus of radius \(r\) and thickness \(\Delta r\), whose area \(2\pi r\,\Delta r\) grows with \(r\), while in the bar there is at each \(r\) only one segment of length \(\Delta r\). In the plane we compute the energy over an area, so \(\varepsilon^2 \propto 1/r\) gives the integral \(\int r^{-1}\,r\,\Delta r\), which is finite.

This remark is not proved in this book. COOK (PDF p. 300) states that quarter-point elements pass the patch test, so as the mesh is refined they approach the solution correctly, and plane elements are introduced in chapter 15. The quarter point is thus at once a defect (for a smooth field: at \(c = 0{,}26\) the strain error is \(18{,}24\) for a largest true strain of \(2\)) and a deliberate tool (for the field \(\sqrt{x}\)), and what decides is the field we are looking for, not the element.

17.5.4 How large should the elements be

We moved a node, now let us move the nodes of the mesh. The tube from the chapter on the boundary value problem (inner radius \(a = 40\) mm, outer \(b = 60\) mm) has by theorem 11.28 the radial displacement \(u(r) = C_1 r + C_2/r\) with second derivative \(u'' = 2C_2/r^3\). At \(r = 40\) mm it is \((60/40)^3 = 3{,}4\) times larger than at \(r = 60\) mm. A uniform mesh has the same element length everywhere, so a large error at the inner edge and a small one at the outer. Can we reach a smaller largest error with the same number of elements? The measure of error is given by lemma 6.40: on an element of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) the error of linear interpolation is at most \(\tfrac18 h_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \mu_{\mathrm{e}}\), where \(\mu_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the largest \(|u''|\) on the element. The measure says how well the mesh can follow the field, not what the error of the solution is (that was stated in section 17.3).

Figure 17.46 shows how a mesh \(B\) with a smaller largest bound would fail to cover the interval. At the top are the nodes \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) of mesh \(A\), below them the nodes \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) of mesh \(B\). The proof shows that every \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies left of \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\), because otherwise the \(k\)th element of mesh \(B\) would contain the \(k\)th element of mesh \(A\). At the last step the node \(s_{\mathrm{n}}\) cannot lie left of \(r_{\mathrm{n}} = b\), since \(s_{\mathrm{n}} = b\).

Lemma 17.26 A mesh with equal bounds (mreža z enakimi mejami)

Let \(u\) have a continuous second derivative on \([a, b]\) and let \(u'' \neq 0\) everywhere. For a mesh \(a = r_0 < r_1 < \dots < r_{\mathrm{n}} = b\) with element lengths \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = r_{\mathrm{e}} - r_{\mathrm{e}-1}\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{e}} = \max |u''|\) on \([r_{\mathrm{e}-1}, r_{\mathrm{e}}]\), let \(\beta_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac18 h_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \mu_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the bound from lemma 6.40, point 2, and \(\beta = \max_{\mathrm{e}} \beta_{\mathrm{e}}\). If there is a mesh \(A\) with \(n\) elements in which all bounds are equal, \(\beta_{\mathrm{e}} = \beta_{\mathrm{A}}\), then no other mesh with \(n\) elements has a smaller largest bound.

Proof

We must show that a mesh with a smaller largest bound would mean that \(n\) elements do not cover the interval.

  1. Let a mesh \(B\) with nodes \(s_0 = a, \dots, s_{\mathrm{n}} = b\) have the largest bound \(\beta_{\mathrm{B}} < \beta_{\mathrm{A}}\).
  2. We claim \(s_{\mathrm{k}} < r_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(k = 1, \dots, n\). For \(k = 1\): if \(s_1 \ge r_1\), the first element of mesh \(B\) would contain the first element of mesh \(A\), so it would have \(h \ge h_1^A\) and \(\mu \ge \mu_1^A\) (the maximum over a larger interval is not smaller), hence \(\beta_1^B \ge \beta_{\mathrm{A}}\), a contradiction. Figure 17.47 shows such a pair: the first element of the uniform mesh, \(2{,}5\) mm long, contains the first element of the mesh with equal bounds, \(1{,}906\) mm long, and its bound \(1{,}22\) is larger than \(0{,}71\).
  3. Let \(s_{\mathrm{k}-1} < r_{\mathrm{k}-1}\). If \(s_{\mathrm{k}} \ge r_{\mathrm{k}}\), the element \(k\) of mesh \(B\) would contain \([r_{\mathrm{k}-1}, r_{\mathrm{k}}]\), again \(\beta_{\mathrm{k}}^B \ge \beta_{\mathrm{k}}^A = \beta_{\mathrm{A}}\), a contradiction. So \(s_{\mathrm{k}} < r_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. For \(k = n\) we get \(s_{\mathrm{n}} < r_{\mathrm{n}} = b\), which contradicts \(s_{\mathrm{n}} = b\).

Source: The proof is not from the source.

The two assumptions of the lemma. The continuous second derivative is needed by lemma 6.40, from which the bound comes. The condition \(u'' \neq 0\) does not enter the proof. It ensures that \(\mu_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) on every element, so that every bound is positive and strictly grows as the element is lengthened, which is why the mesh with equal bounds can be built step by step. For a loaded tube it holds, because \(u'' = 2C_2/r^3\) and \(C_2 \neq 0\). It does not hold for a field with an inflection or a straight piece, for example at \(C_2 = 0\), where \(u = C_1 r\), the bound is zero for every mesh and the lemma says nothing.

Example 17.27 Tube with eight elements (cev z osmimi elementi)

On \([40, 60]\) mm the \(|u''|\) is decreasing, so \(\mu_{\mathrm{e}} = |u''|\) at the left end of the element. The uniform mesh has \(h = 2{,}5\) mm and bounds from \(1{,}22\cdot 10^{-5}\,C\) at the inner edge to \(0{,}41\cdot 10^{-5}\,C\) at the outer, where \(C = 2|C_2|\). The mesh with equal bounds (step by step from \(r_0 = 40\) mm, SymPy and NumPy) has nodes at \(40\), \(41{,}906\), \(43{,}950\), \(46{,}146\), \(48{,}508\), \(51{,}054\), \(53{,}803\), \(56{,}776\) and \(60\) mm, elements between \(1{,}906\) and \(3{,}224\) mm, and everywhere the bound \(0{,}71\cdot 10^{-5}\,C\). The largest bound is \(1{,}72\) times smaller than for the uniform mesh (at \(n = 4\): \(1{,}59\) times, at \(n = 16\): \(1{,}79\) times). Figure 17.47 shows this above the radius \(r\) from \(40\) to \(60\) mm: for the uniform mesh the columns have different heights, for gradually larger elements all are equal and below the dashed level of the first mesh.

A test that limits the lemma: neighbouring elements differ by a factor from \(1{,}072\) to \(1{,}084\), so the change of size is not abrupt (COOK, PDF p. 355: abrupt changes of size are not recommended because they cause a disturbance in the field of gradients). But the bound is a measure for displacements. For the strain (the derivative, which in section 17.4 gives us the stress), point 1 of lemma 6.40 gives the bound \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\mu_{\mathrm{e}}\), and equal bounds require elements \(h_{\mathrm{e}} \propto 1/\mu_{\mathrm{e}}\) from \(1{,}498\) to \(4{,}090\) mm, a ratio of \(2{,}73\) instead of \(1{,}69\). A mesh adapted to displacements is therefore not the best for stresses: neighbouring elements differ at the strain bound by a factor of up to \(1{,}21\), and the mesh for displacements has a \(1{,}27\) times larger strain bound than the mesh for strains (the bounds are \(2{,}98\cdot 10^{-5}\,C\) and \(2{,}34\cdot 10^{-5}\,C\), the uniform mesh has \(3{,}91\cdot 10^{-5}\,C\)).

17.5.5 Plane and space

Everything we proved is one-dimensional. In the plane the element map is \((\xi, \eta) \mapsto (x, y)\), its derivative is a \(2 \times 2\) matrix and its determinant is the Jacobian determinant (chapter 15). The reasons are the same: changing the variable in an integral and in the strain needs an invertible map, that is a determinant that is nowhere zero. Figure 17.48 shows six shapes of a quadrilateral element that COOK lists as shapes that as a rule reduce accuracy (section 10.3, PDF pp. 354 to 355, section 6.11, PDF p. 250). Each time a good square is drawn next to it. The elongated element has a large aspect ratio \(a/b\), the skewed one has an angle \(\alpha\) far from \(90^\circ\), the tapered one has parallel sides \(a\) and \(b\) of different lengths, and the node on a side is moved off the centre, like our \(c\). The curved side has a sag \(s\). In the last element a corner is pushed over the diagonal between its neighbouring corners, so the angle at it is larger than \(180^\circ\) and \(J < 0\) there, as in our \(c < \tfrac14\).

What does this mean for the choice of mesh? COOK states: computed results are most accurate for compact elements with straight sides, and larger elongation, non-orthogonality, curvature of sides and offset of side nodes as a rule reduce accuracy (PDF p. 250), distortion spoils gradients, that is stresses, more than displacements, natural frequencies or temperatures (PDF p. 354), and the amount of spoiling depends on the kind of element, the arrangement of the mesh and the physical problem (ibid.), so there is no limit that would hold for all. An eight-node element loses exact bending if the angle departs from \(90^\circ\), the sides are curved or the side nodes are not at the midpoints (PDF p. 250), which is the plane version of our case \(c \ne \tfrac12\). An element with \(J < 0\) at some Gauss point is not acceptable, and programs check the shapes of the elements before the computation and may refuse to compute until the bad shapes are corrected (PDF p. 250). Mesh quality is thus two things: the shape of a single element (a checkable property, \(J > 0\) and reasonably constant) and the arrangement of sizes (lemma 17.26, abrupt changes are bad). For three-dimensional elements the warping of faces is added (COOK, PDF p. 355), here it is only named. How programs generate a mesh (advancing front, Delaunay triangulation) we do not treat here.

This section treated the discretization error. What the shape of the elements does to it we showed on the bar: moving the middle node from the centre does not change the number of elements, but at \(c = 0{,}26\) it makes the strain error \(9\) times the largest true strain, while the mesh with equal bounds lowers the largest bound \(1{,}72\) times with the same number of elements. The model error (\(c\) changed nothing in the model of the bar) and the numerical error (the conditioning of the stiffness matrix at small \(J\), treated in the section on large systems of equations) remain.

17.6 Large systems of equations and numerical error (veliki sistemi enačb in številčna napaka)

The mesh is chosen, the elements are good, and one computation remains: the system \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) whose matrix has a thousand or a million rows. This section treats the third of the three errors of definition 17.2, the numerical error (številčna napaka). The computer stores every number with about \(16\) significant digits (double precision, as in chapter 6) and every operation rounds, by a relative amount of about \(10^{-16}\). Reducing the modelling and the discretization error does not reduce this error, and may even increase it. A finer mesh reduces the discretization error (section 17.3) but raises the order \(n\) of the system and with it the cost of the computation. COOK (PDF p. 318, read) says that great mesh refinement, meant to decrease the discretization error, may increase the numerical error to such an extent that the results become less accurate rather than more. We ask three questions. What does one system cost, and what does each further system with the same matrix cost? How many digits do we lose for the bar of chapter 7 as the mesh is refined? And when does a large condition number really spoil the solution, and when does it not?

17.6.1 One factorization, many right-hand sides

Chapter 7 (section 7.8) showed that a banded matrix with half-bandwidth \(b\) costs about \(n b^2/2\) multiplications in elimination instead of \(n^3/6\) (lemma 7.44), and that renumbering the unknowns changes the band but not the solution (lemma 7.46). We do not repeat this, figure 7.99 shows the difference. Take the same example: a mesh of \(50 \times 100\) nodes with two unknowns per node, so \(n = 10^4\) and \(b = 100\), and the cost of the factorization is \(n b^2/2 = 5 \cdot 10^7\) multiplications. The question that practice asks is not answered there. We load the same structure in several ways (own weight, wind from the left, wind from the right), and in a vibration computation by the trapezoidal rule (definition 10.92) we solve a system at every time step, and for a given time step its matrix does not depend on the step (chapter 10). Does every new right-hand side cost another \(5 \cdot 10^7\) multiplications?

No, and the reason lies in what elimination does. The multipliers with which elimination subtracts rows depend only on the matrix, not on the right-hand side. The factor \(\mat L\) stores them (lemma 7.47), so the work on the matrix is done once, and for a new right-hand side we repeat only the subtractions on it. We count them on the figure.

On the left is the factor \(\mat L\), a square with \(n\) rows and its diagonal. The nonzero entries are only in the band below the diagonal, which is \(b\) entries high, and elsewhere there are zeros. Row \(i\) therefore has at most \(b\) entries to the left of the diagonal. The solution comes in three passes: from the top down we compute \(\vek y\), along the diagonal \(\vek z\) and from the bottom up \(\vek d\). Below each pass is its cost, which the lemma proves.

Lemma 17.28 Cost of one further right-hand side (cena ene nadaljnje desne strani)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\) with half-bandwidth \(b\) (definition 7.40) and \(\mat K = \mat L\,\mat D\,\mat L^\T\) its factorization from lemma 7.47. Then:

  1. \(L_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) for \(i - j > b\), that is, zeros outside the band.
  2. For every column \(\vek f\) with \(n\) entries we solve \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) by a forward pass, a division by the diagonal and a backward pass, and this costs at most \(2nb + n\) multiplications and divisions once the factorization is computed.
Proof

We must show that the factor \(\mat L\) has a band and that the solution takes three simple passes. Write \(\vek y = \mat D\,\mat L^\T\vek d\) and \(\vek z = \mat L^\T\vek d\).

  1. Column \(k\) of \(\mat L\) below the diagonal is the column of multipliers \(\vek g/K_{11}^{(k)}\) of the \(k\)-th elimination step (lemma 7.47). By lemma 7.42 the matrix \(\mat K^{(k)}\) has half-bandwidth at most \(b\), so in its first column \(g_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for \(i > b + 1\) (step 3 of the proof of lemma 7.42). Column \(k\) of \(\mat L\) therefore has nonzero entries only in the first \(b\) places below the diagonal, which is item 1.
  2. We split the equation \(\mat L\,\mat D\,\mat L^\T\vek d = \vek f\) into three: \(\mat L\,\vek y = \vek f\), \(\mat D\,\vek z = \vek y\) and \(\mat L^\T\vek d = \vek z\).
  3. The first equation has a lower triangular matrix with ones on the diagonal: \(y_{\mathrm{i}} = f_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{j} < \mathrm{i}} L_{\mathrm{ij}}\,y_{\mathrm{j}}\). By step 1 the sum has at most \(b\) terms, so at most \(b\) multiplications per row and \(n b\) in all, and no divisions.
  4. The second equation is \(n\) divisions, \(z_{\mathrm{i}} = y_{\mathrm{i}}/D_{\mathrm{ii}}\), with pivots \(D_{\mathrm{ii}} > 0\) (theorem 6.29).
  5. The third has an upper triangular matrix with ones: \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = z_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{j} > \mathrm{i}} L_{\mathrm{ji}}\,d_{\mathrm{j}}\), again at most \(b\) terms per row and \(n b\) multiplications, because row \(i\) of \(\mat L^\T\) is column \(i\) of \(\mat L\).
  6. The sum of steps 3, 4 and 5 is at most \(2nb + n\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources.

On the example that the right part of figure 17.49 shows: \(n = 10^4\) and \(b = 100\) give \(2nb + n = 2{,}01 \cdot 10^6\) multiplications for one right-hand side, while the factorization costs \(5 \cdot 10^7\). The ratio is \(24{,}9\), in general \((n b^2/2)/(2nb) = b/4\). On the axes are the number of right-hand sides \(N\) and the number of multiplications \(N_{\mathrm{op}}\), both on logarithmic scales. The blackwhite straight line is the cost when the factorization is repeated for every right-hand side, the orange curve the cost with a single factorization. The factorization dominates until there are about \(b/4 = 25\) right-hand sides: up to there the orange curve hardly rises. For \(100\) right-hand sides, repeating the factorization costs \(5{,}2 \cdot 10^9\) multiplications, one factorization and \(100\) solutions \(2{,}5 \cdot 10^8\), which is \(20{,}7\) times less, and for \(1000\) time steps \(25\) times less (\(5{,}2 \cdot 10^{10}\) against \(2{,}06 \cdot 10^9\)). The numbers are in num-06.out. This is what chapter 10 promises when it says that the factorization is made once and only applied at every step.

This saving has a limit that we see on the same example. With a single right-hand side the factorization saves nothing, the ratio is \(1{,}00\), where the two curves start at the same point. The matrix also changes when we change the time step \(\Delta t\), because it contains it, and then the factorization must be computed again. If that happens at every step, we are back on the blackwhite straight line. In a nonlinear computation the matrix changes at every correction, as we shall see in later sections of this chapter, so there the factorization is not free. Lemma 17.28 therefore holds for the same matrix and many right-hand sides, not for many matrices.

Band storage is not the only one. COOK (PDF pp. 57-58, read) stores, for a symmetric matrix, in one array all entries from the topmost nonzero entry of each column down to the diagonal (the skyline, obris) and all the zeros between them, because a direct solver turns the zeros under the skyline into nonzero entries (fill, zapolnitev). The number of stored entries is the profile of the matrix. For the same mesh one numbering gives a profile of \(21\), another \(39\), and programs renumber by themselves. The frontal method (čelni postopek) alternates assembly and solution, so that only the part of the matrix still needed by the front that travels across the structure is in memory at one time. Iterative solvers produce no fill, but converge more slowly as the condition number grows, and use preconditioning (predpogojevanje). The book does not treat these methods and names them only because a program offers a choice between them. For the bar we compute the condition number now.

17.6.2 How many digits we lose for the bar

The condition number \(\kappa(\mat K) = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) (definition 6.31) tells by how much a relative error of the right-hand side can grow in the solution, and chapter 6 estimated this as \(|\delta\vek x|/|\vek x| \le \kappa\,|\delta\vek b|/|\vek b|\). For hat functions on a bar with \(n = 4\), \(8\) and \(16\) equal elements it gave \(\kappa = 29\), \(113\) and \(438\) (matrix (6.15)), about \(1{,}7\,n^2\). Why a square, and does it still hold at \(n = 1000\)?

Take the same bar: constant cross-section \(EA\), length \(L\), clamped at \(x = 0\), free at \(x = L\), divided into \(n\) equal elements of length \(h = L/n\). The unknowns are the nodal displacements \(d_1, \dots, d_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the stiffness matrix is \(\mat K = (EA/h)\,\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) with the matrix

\[\mat T_{\mathrm{n}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & & & \\ -1 & 2 & -1 & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ & & & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{17.21}\]

in which the empty places are zeros. The number \(EA/h\) only multiplies all eigenvalues, so \(\kappa(\mat K) = \kappa(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}})\). Let us look at the condition number of \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) in figure 17.50, on logarithmic scales, and next to it the shapes that the matrix at \(n = 10\) moves most and least.

First the axes: horizontally the number of elements \(n\), vertically the condition number \(\kappa\), both on logarithmic scales, because we care how many times it grows and not by how much. On the dashed straight line lies \((4n/\pi)^2\) and its slope is \(2\), which means that \(\kappa\) grows a hundredfold for ten times more elements. The points are the exact values of the matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) and lie on the line. Why slope \(2\)? On the right the left edge is the wall in which the bar is clamped. Above is the softest shape of the matrix \(\mat T_{10}\), a smooth curve: the differences \(v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) between neighbouring displacements are small (the thick dash is one of them), so the ratio \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} (v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}-1})^2/\sum_{\mathrm{k}} v_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) of element stretches to displacements is small, and this ratio is the eigenvalue (since \(\vek v^\T\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} (v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}-1})^2\) with \(v_0 = 0\)), here \(\lambda_1 = 0{,}0223\). Below is the stiffest shape, in which neighbouring nodes move oppositely and the stretch of every element is the largest possible for the given displacements, with the eigenvalue \(\lambda_{10} = 3{,}9111\). At the free end both shapes carry one more node, drawn empty, at the same height as the last one: to the right of the last node there is no element to stretch, and the proof will write this as \(v_{\mathrm{n}+1} = v_{\mathrm{n}}\).

Why does the smallest eigenvalue fall with \(n\)? With more elements the same smooth curve is cut into more and shorter steps, so each difference is proportional to \(1/n\) and its square to \(1/n^2\). Why does the largest stay below \(4\)? For any two numbers \((v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}-1})^2 \le 2v_{\mathrm{k}}^2 + 2v_{\mathrm{k}-1}^2\), so the sum of the squared stretches does not exceed four times the sum of the squared displacements, and the stiffest shape comes close to this bound. Their ratio is the condition number. Let us look at it exactly.

Lemma 17.29 Condition number of the bar (število občutljivosti palice)

Let \(n \ge 1\), let \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the matrix (17.21) of order \(n\) of a clamped and free bar and \(\theta = \pi/\big(2(2n + 1)\big)\). Then:

  1. The matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} = 4\sin^2\!\big((2j - 1)\theta\big)\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\) and an eigenvector \(\vek v^{(j)}\) with entries \(v^{(j)}_{\mathrm{k}} = \sin\!\big((2j - 1)\,k\,\pi/(2n + 1)\big)\).
  2. The condition number is
    \[\kappa(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}) = \frac{\sin^2\!\big((2n - 1)\theta\big)}{\sin^2\theta} = \frac{\cos^2\!\big(\pi/(2n + 1)\big)}{\sin^2\theta} . \tag{17.22}\]
  3. For every \(n\) the condition number lies between bounds around the dashed line:
    \[\Big(\frac{2(2n + 1)}{\pi}\Big)^2 \cos^2\frac{\pi}{2n + 1} \le \kappa(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}) \le \Big(\frac{2(2n + 1)}{\pi}\Big)^2 \frac{1}{(1 - \theta/2)^2} . \tag{17.23}\]
Proof

We must show that the listed vectors solve the eigenvalue problem, that these are all the eigenvalues, and that equation (17.22) and the estimate (17.23) follow. Write \(\varphi = (2j - 1)\pi/(2n + 1)\), so that \(v_{\mathrm{k}} = \sin k\varphi\), and also \(v_0 = 0\) and \(v_{\mathrm{n}+1} = v_{\mathrm{n}}\).

  1. Row \(k\) of \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) for \(1 \le k \le n - 1\) gives \(-v_{\mathrm{k}-1} + 2v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) (at \(k = 1\) we have \(v_0 = 0\), which is the clamp). Row \(n\) gives \(-v_{\mathrm{n}-1} + v_{\mathrm{n}}\), which is the same form with \(v_{\mathrm{n}+1} = v_{\mathrm{n}}\) (free end: the last element has no right neighbour).
  2. By the addition formulas (corollary 8.16) \(\sin(k - 1)\varphi + \sin(k + 1)\varphi = 2\sin k\varphi\,\cos\varphi\), so \(-v_{\mathrm{k}-1} + 2v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}+1} = (2 - 2\cos\varphi)\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\). Since by the same theorem \(\cos\varphi = 1 - 2\sin^2(\varphi/2)\), we have \(2 - 2\cos\varphi = 4\sin^2(\varphi/2)\).
  3. The condition \(v_{\mathrm{n}+1} = v_{\mathrm{n}}\) holds, because by the addition formulas \(\sin(n + 1)\varphi - \sin n\varphi = 2\cos\!\big((n + \tfrac12)\varphi\big)\sin\tfrac{\varphi}{2}\) and \((n + \tfrac12)\varphi = (2j - 1)\pi/2\), where the cosine is zero.
  4. The vector \(\vek v^{(j)}\) is not zero, since \(v_1 = \sin\varphi \ne 0\) for \(0 < \varphi < \pi\). So \(4\sin^2(\varphi/2) = 4\sin^2\!\big((2j - 1)\theta\big)\) is an eigenvalue. The angle \((2j - 1)\theta\) lies in \((0, \pi/2)\), where \(\sin^2\) is strictly increasing, so these \(n\) values are pairwise different. A matrix of order \(n\) has at most \(n\) eigenvalues, so these are all. This is item 1.
  5. By the increase the smallest eigenvalue is at \(j = 1\) and the largest at \(j = n\), and their ratio is the first part of equation (17.22). Since \((2n - 1)\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2} - \tfrac{\pi}{2n + 1}\), we have \(\sin\!\big((2n - 1)\theta\big) = \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2n + 1}\) (addition formula), which is the second part.
  6. The estimate: by theorem 8.68 for \(\sin\) with the second derivative \(\sin\theta = \theta - \tfrac12\,\theta^2\sin\xi\) with \(0 < \xi < \theta\), so \(\theta - \theta^2/2 \le \sin\theta \le \theta\). The upper bound gives the lower bound in (17.23), since \(1/\theta^2 = (2(2n + 1)/\pi)^2\), the lower bound gives the upper one, since \(\cos^2 \le 1\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. That the condition number of an axially loaded bar grows with the square of the number of elements is stated by COOK (PDF p. 322, read, exponent \(2m/n = 2/1\)), and the lemma proves it for this bar.

The lemma says what the figure shows. The largest eigenvalue is below \(4\) and approaches it, the smallest is \(4\sin^2\theta\), about \(\pi^2/(2n + 1)^2\), so it falls as \(1/n^2\). The ratio is therefore about \((4n/\pi)^2\), and the slope \(2\) is the slope of this expression. For \(n = 4\), \(8\) and \(16\) the lemma gives \(29{,}28\), \(113{,}50\) and \(437{,}70\) (points in the figure), exactly the \(29\), \(113\) and \(438\) of chapter 6. For larger \(n\):

\(100\) \(16\,370{,}2\) \(16\,369{,}9\) \(16\,502{,}6\) \(1{,}010\) \(4{,}2\)
\(1000\) \(1\,622\,757\) \(1\,622\,756\) \(1\,624\,035\) \(1{,}001\) \(6{,}2\)

The last column is the estimate of the lost digits. Why exactly \(\log_{10}\kappa\)?

Let us draw a number in the computer as \(16\) cells, one for each digit, in part (a) of the figure. Rounding spoils the last cell, relatively by \(10^{-16}\). The estimate of chapter 6 says that the relative error of the solution can be \(\kappa\) times larger. For the bar of \(1000\) elements \(\kappa = 10^{6{,}2}\), so \(10^{-16} \cdot 10^{6{,}2} = 10^{-9{,}8}\), and multiplying by \(10^{6{,}2}\) is a shift by \(6{,}2\) cells to the left. That many cells can be spoiled, the other \(16 - 6{,}2 = 9{,}8\) are reliable, almost ten. COOK (PDF p. 321, read) says the same: with \(d\) digits in a computer number \(d_{\text{acc}} \ge d - \log_{10}\kappa\) digits are accurate, and the sign \(\ge\) means that \(\log_{10}\kappa\) may overestimate the loss, which we shall see in the next section. For a bar, refining the mesh does no harm. For a beam, however, COOK (PDF p. 322, read) gives the exponent \(2m/n = 4/1\), where \(2m\) is the order of the highest displacement derivative in the differential equation, \(2\) for the bar and \(4\) for the beam: \(\kappa\) grows with the fourth power of the number of elements, and doubling them increases it \(16\) times. That is \(\log_{10}16 = 1{,}2\) digits more at every doubling, for the bar only \(\log_{10}4 = 0{,}6\) digits. For a beam, refining a mesh that reduces the discretization error therefore quickly raises the numerical one.

17.6.3 When a large condition number is harmful

The condition number is an upper estimate, not a prediction, as the true error shows. COOK (PDF p. 316, read) says that we cannot call a matrix ill-conditioned (slabo pogojena) until we state what is done with it: a matrix that is good for solving equations can be bad for eigenvalues and vice versa. The simplest example where this shows is two springs in a chain.

We set up the model. A spring of stiffness \(k_1\) is fixed to the wall, at its other end is node 1, then follows a spring of stiffness \(k_2\) and node 2, where the force \(F\) pulls. The springs are linear, massless and frictionless, and the displacements are small, so that the nodes stay on one straight line (an idealization that chapter 7 also uses). We draw the soft spring \(k_1\) as a long coil and the stiff spring \(k_2\) as a short, thick coil, because that is exactly the difference we care about. A linear spring pulls with a force equal to stiffness times stretch, which holds as long as it returns to its original length when unloaded. Without this the matrix would not have constant entries. At rest, mass and friction give no force along the chain, so we leave them out without error. The displacement \(u_1\) is the distance between the original position of node 1 and its position after loading, the displacement \(u_2\) the same for node 2. When we measure off \(u_1\) from \(u_2\), a short blue piece \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = u_2 - u_1\) remains, the stretch of the stiff spring.

We write the equilibrium conditions as always, on free bodies. On node 1 the left spring pulls back with the force \(k_1 u_1\) and the right one forward with the force \(k_2(u_2 - u_1)\), because the right spring is stretched by \(u_2 - u_1\). With no external force \(k_1 u_1 = k_2(u_2 - u_1)\). On node 2 the force \(F\) pulls forward and the right spring back with the force \(k_2(u_2 - u_1)\), so \(k_2(u_2 - u_1) = F\). In matrix form

\[\begin{bmatrix} k_1 + k_2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ F \end{bmatrix} . \tag{17.24}\]

The solution is \(u_1 = F/k_1\) and \(u_2 = F/k_1 + F/k_2\), which we check by substituting into both equations. Let \(k_1 = 1\) and \(F = 1\) (displacements in the unit \(F/k_1\)), \(s = k_2/k_1\) the stiffness ratio, so the true displacement is \(u_2 = 1 + 1/s\). In elimination without row exchange the pivot is \(k_1 + k_2\) and the second row after the first step has the coefficient \(k_2 - k_2^2/(k_1 + k_2) = k_1 k_2/(k_1 + k_2)\). The information about \(k_1\) is hidden in this difference in the last digits of the number \(k_2\): at \(s = 10^{15}\) and \(16\) digits only one of them remains. Part (b) of figure 17.51 shows this. The stiffness \(k_2 = 10^{15}\) fills all \(16\) cells, \(k_1 = 1\) lands in the last one, and in the sum \(k_1 + k_2\), which is the pivot, the soft spring has a single cell. The further digits of \(k_1\) have no cell and are lost in the addition.

Lemma 17.30 Stiff spring on a soft one (toga vzmet na mehki)

Let \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) be positive, \(s = k_2/k_1\) and let \(\mat K\) be the matrix of equation (17.24). Then:

  1. The condition number \(\kappa\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is the larger solution of the equation \(\kappa + 1/\kappa = 4s + 2 + 1/s\) and
    \[4s + 1 + \frac1s < \kappa < 4s + 2 + \frac1s . \tag{17.25}\]
  2. For the unknowns \(u_1\) and \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = u_2 - u_1\) the matrix of the system is \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}} = \mathrm{diag}(k_1, k_2)\) and the right-hand side \((F, F)^\T\), so \(\kappa(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}}) = s\) and the solution is \(u_1 = F/k_1\), \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = F/k_2\), each with one division.
Proof

We must show the equation for \(\kappa\) and the form of the second matrix. The first item needs the trace and the determinant, the second the energy of the springs.

  1. The eigenvalues are the roots of the equation
    \[\lambda^2 - (k_1 + 2k_2)\lambda + k_1 k_2 = 0 ,\]
    since the trace is \(k_1 + 2k_2\) and the determinant is \((k_1 + k_2)k_2 - k_2^2 = k_1 k_2\). The discriminant \(k_1^2 + 4k_2^2\) is positive, the sum and product of the roots are positive, so both are positive and distinct.
  2. From \((\lambda_{\max} + \lambda_{\min})^2/(\lambda_{\max}\lambda_{\min}) = \kappa + 2 + 1/\kappa\) and step 1 we get \(\kappa + 2 + 1/\kappa = (k_1 + 2k_2)^2/(k_1 k_2) = 4s + 4 + 1/s\). Hence \(\kappa + 1/\kappa = 4s + 2 + 1/s\).
  3. Since the eigenvalues are distinct, \(\kappa > 1\) and \(0 < 1/\kappa < 1\). From step 2 it follows that \(\kappa < 4s + 2 + 1/s\) and \(\kappa > 4s + 1 + 1/s\).
  4. The second item. The soft spring is stretched by \(u_1\), the stiff one by \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the force does work on the displacement \(u_2\). The potential energy is therefore \(\Pi = \tfrac12 k_1 u_1^2 + \tfrac12 k_2 u_{\mathrm{r}}^2 - F u_2\) and \(u_2 = u_1 + u_{\mathrm{r}}\). By stationarity (corollary 8.63) the equations are \(\partial\Pi/\partial u_1 = k_1 u_1 - F = 0\) and \(\partial\Pi/\partial u_{\mathrm{r}} = k_2 u_{\mathrm{r}} - F = 0\), which is a diagonal system with the matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(k_1, k_2)\) and the right-hand side \((F, F)^\T\). The eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, the ratio is \(k_2/k_1 = s\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK (PDF pp. 316-317, read) uses the same two-spring chain to explain ill-conditioning, there with \(k_1 \gg k_2\) and different notation. The relative degrees of freedom (PDF pp. 319-320) are the same idea as item 2.

The numbers for \(k_1 = 1\) (num-06.out, in agreement with c17.out) are the orange points, the dashed line and the open circles of the figure:

\(s\) \(\kappa\) (lemma) error of \(u_2\) with \((u_1, u_2)\) \(4s \cdot 10^{-16}\) error of \(u_2\) with \((u_1, u_{\mathrm{r}})\)
\(10^3\) \(4{,}002 \cdot 10^3\) \(5{,}8 \cdot 10^{-14}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-13}\) below \(10^{-16}\)
\(10^6\) \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^6\) \(8{,}6 \cdot 10^{-12}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-10}\) below \(10^{-16}\)
\(10^9\) \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^9\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-7}\) below \(10^{-16}\)
\(10^{12}\) \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^{12}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-4}\) below \(10^{-16}\)
\(10^{15}\) \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^{15}\) \(1{,}4 \cdot 10^{-1}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-1}\) below \(10^{-16}\)

The same numbers are on the right of figure 17.52. On the axes are the stiffness ratio \(s\) horizontally and the relative error \(\varepsilon\) of the displacement \(u_2\) vertically, both on logarithmic scales, because both change by many orders of magnitude. The column \(\kappa\) says that \(\kappa \approx 4k_2/k_1\). At \(s = 10^{15}\) NumPy gives \(4{,}571 \cdot 10^{15}\) from the computed eigenvalues instead of the \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^{15}\) of the lemma (num-06.out). The smallest eigenvalue there is about \(0{,}5\), while the entries of the matrix are about \(10^{15}\), so rounding spoils it already in the computation of the eigenvalues. The column with the error for the unknowns \((u_1, u_2)\) is the displacement error measured on the computer (with the NumPy library), in the figure the orange line. It stays below the estimate \(4s \cdot 10^{-16} \approx \kappa \cdot 10^{-16}\) of the column after it, in the figure the dashed straight line, and follows it: from \(s = 10^3\) to \(s = 10^{15}\) both grow by about \(12\) orders of magnitude. At \(s = 10^{15}\) the error is \(14\) %, the last orange point just below \(10^0\), and the result is useless, while the same system in other unknowns stays accurate. The last column, in the figure the empty blue circles, is a case where a large condition number does not mean a loss: the matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(1, s)\) has \(\kappa = s\), a quarter of the number of the matrix \(\mat K\), but loses no digit, because it contains no subtraction of nearly equal numbers. The condition number is therefore an upper estimate of the loss, not a prediction.

Two more cases show what a large condition number says and what it does not.

On the figure every eigenvalue is a point on the horizontal axis, divided by powers of ten, because we care about the ratio, and this is a distance here. In the top group are the eigenvalues of \(\mat T_{10}\) and the distance between them, \(\log_{10}\kappa = 2{,}2\). Below are the same values multiplied by \(1000\): both move three decades to the right and the distance stays. In the middle group are the eigenvalues of \(\mat K\) at \(s = 10^6\) and the eigenvalues of the matrix with ones on the diagonal, where they move differently and the distance \(6{,}6\) stays. In the bottom group are the eigenvalues of \(\mathrm{diag}(1, s)\) and, after equalizing the diagonal, both at \(1\), the distance is zero.

  • Multiply the whole matrix by \(1000\), for example by changing from N/mm to N/m. All eigenvalues are multiplied by \(1000\) and the ratio is the same: for \(\mat T_{10}\) we have \(\kappa = 175{,}0866\) before and after. A change of units in all equations at once therefore causes no bad conditioning and cures none. It is different with a change of unknowns, such as from \((u_1, u_2)\) to \((u_1, u_{\mathrm{r}})\). COOK (PDF p. 320, read) therefore proposes to compute \(\kappa\) from the matrix multiplied by a diagonal matrix so that it has ones on the diagonal, because it is then large only when the matrix is really nearly singular. For \(\mat K\) of equation (17.24) this is the matrix \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -r \\ -r & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) with \(r = \sqrt{s/(1 + s)}\), eigenvalues \(1 \pm r\) and ratio \((1 + r)/(1 - r) \approx 4s\), as large as before. For \(\mathrm{diag}(1, s)\) the same procedure gives the unit matrix and \(\kappa = 1\).
  • Load the springs differently: the force \(F\) pulls node 1 back and node 2 forward, so \(\vek f = (-F, F)^\T\), two equal and opposite forces at the ends of the stiff spring, in equilibrium together. At \(s = 10^{12}\) and \(10^{15}\) the computed stretch \(u_2 - u_1\) equals \(10^{-12}\) and \(10^{-15}\) (num-06.out), although the matrix is the same and \(\kappa\) equally large. COOK (PDF p. 317) says that under an equilibrium load the relative displacement is computed accurately even if the rigid displacement carries an error. The error is in the displacement of the whole stiff mass, not in the stretch of the spring.

When, then, do we expect trouble? When a stiff mass sits on a soft support and we care about a displacement or a force that the soft support determines (COOK, PDF p. 317, read): the information about the soft support is in the last digits of the stiff terms. A similar phenomenon is in chapter 12, where the penalty stiffness of a constraint makes \(\kappa\) grow at least as the penalty number (lemma 12.29), and in shear locking, where the stiffness of the element itself does this. Lemma 12.29 is not used here, because the matrix without the stiff spring would have to be positive definite, and the soft spring at the wall does not hold \(u_2\) at all. The kinship is therefore in the mechanism and not in the theorem. The remedy is the same as there. COOK (PDF pp. 319-320, read) names it: we choose the unknowns so that the large number does not appear off the diagonal, as \(u_1\) and \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) above, or with local axes at an inclined support.

17.6.4 What we showed

This section treated only the numerical error, the third of the three, and it does not reduce the modelling or the discretization error. The factorization is computed once and every further right-hand side costs \(2nb + n\) instead of \(n b^2/2\) (lemma 17.28), but only for the same matrix. The condition number of the bar grows as \((4n/\pi)^2\) (lemma 17.29), for a beam by COOK as \(n^4\), so a refinement that reduces the discretization error raises the numerical one. A large condition number is an upper estimate of the loss of digits: a stiff spring on a soft one has it and also suffers the loss (lemma 17.30, \(\kappa \approx 4k_2/k_1\)), the same system in relative unknowns has the number \(s\), a quarter of it, and no loss. For every result we therefore ask three questions: how much modelling error, how much discretization error and how many digits we have lost.

17.7 Nonlinear statics and imperfections

So far the model has always been linear: displacements are proportional to the load, the stiffness matrix is constant and one system of equations gives the answer. Section 17.1 set the modelling error beside the discretization error and the numerical error (definition 17.2). Here we meet the case where the linear model itself is wrong. The section treats the modelling error and the numerical error that a stopped iteration causes in a nonlinear model. It does not treat the discretization error, because we take models with one unknown and so there is no mesh. Reducing one error does not reduce the others: a Newton iteration that runs to the eighth decimal place does not repair a model that is wrong. The section answers three questions. What is different in a nonlinear model compared with a linear one? How do we solve an equation that cannot be solved directly, and what does the solution we find tell us and not tell us? Why does linear buckling analysis (definition 12.51) predict, for some columns, a load that is never reached?

17.7.1 Two models of a column

We take the simplest column that shows buckling. A rigid bar of length \(L\) is attached at the bottom by a pin, a support that lets the bar only rotate. The bar is rigid, so it does not bend and its position is a single angle \(\theta\) measured from the vertical (angle \(\theta\)). At its top a vertical force \(P\) acts downwards. The force is a load (obremenitev), a force that we apply to the body from outside. It stays vertical even when the bar tilts. A spring holds the bar upright, and we compare two ways of doing it. In model (i) a rotational spring of stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{r}}\) (moment per radian) sits in the pin, as in example 8.74. In model (ii) a horizontal spring of stiffness \(k\) (force per length) joins the top of the bar to a wall. Both springs are linear, only the geometry brings nonlinearity: the angle \(\theta\) enters the equations through \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\). We call such a source geometric nonlinearity (geometrijska nelinearnost), because we write equilibrium on the tilted position, not on the initial one.

A real bar is not perfectly straight, the load is not exactly on the axis and the support is not perfect. We capture these departures with one number: the springs are unstretched at the angle \(\theta_0\), not at \(\theta = 0\), which the dashed position \(\theta_0\) shows in the figure. We call \(\theta_0\) the imperfection (nepopolnost), since a perfect column (\(\theta_0 = 0\)) cannot be reached in any workshop. With \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad the top of a bar of length \(L = 1\) m is displaced from the vertical by \(L\sin\theta_0 = 10{,}00\) mm. This is the size of imperfection we shall compute. The model has three idealizations, each chosen for a reason. The bar is rigid. This is right when the spring is much softer than the bar, since then the bar leans as a whole before it bends noticeably itself. The effect is that one angle \(\theta\) describes the position and one equation the equilibrium. The price is that the model knows nothing of the buckling of the bar itself between the pin and the top. The springs are linear and the spring of model (ii) stays horizontal. This holds as long as the vertical displacement of the top is small against the horizontal one: at \(\theta = 0{,}22\) rad and \(L = 1\) m the top moves sideways by \(L\sin\theta = 218\) mm and down by only \(L(1 - \cos\theta) = 24\) mm. The force \(P\) stays vertical, like the weight of a load resting on the top. A force that turned with the bar would give a different energy of the load and a different computation.

We write the energy of model (ii) as in example 8.74. The horizontal spring is stretched by \(L(\sin\theta - \sin\theta_0)\), because the horizontal distance of the top of the bar from the vertical through the pin is \(L\sin\theta\) and the spring is unstretched in the dashed position, at \(L\sin\theta_0\). The height of the top is \(L\cos\theta\), so the energy of the load \(P\) is \(P L\cos\theta\). With \(s_0 = \sin\theta_0\),

\[V(\theta) = \tfrac12\,k L^2\,(\sin\theta - s_0)^2 + P L\cos\theta . \tag{17.26}\]

Model (i) has \(V = \tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{r}}(\theta - \theta_0)^2 + P L\cos\theta\). By corollary 8.63 equilibrium is a stationary point of the energy, \(V'(\theta) = 0\). By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82) the derivative is \(V' = kL^2(\sin\theta - s_0)\cos\theta - P L\sin\theta\). We write the load as the share \(p = P/(kL)\) of the number \(kL\), which we shall meet at once as the critical load, and divide the derivative by \(kL^2\):

\[g(\theta; p) = \frac{V'(\theta)}{kL^2} = (\sin\theta - s_0)\cos\theta - p\,\sin\theta . \tag{17.27}\]

The number \(g\) tells how much generalized force (with the opposite sign, \(g = -Q/(kL^2)\) by definition 8.58) remains unbalanced on the bar, so we call it the imbalance (neuravnoteženost). Equilibrium is \(g = 0\).

Let us test what nonlinearity changes, on model (ii) with \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad (NumPy). Figure 17.55 has on its axes the angle \(\theta\) across and the share \(p\) up. The grey dashed vertical is the unloaded position \(\theta_0\). The orange curve is the equilibria \(g = 0\) as \(p\) grows from zero. At \(p = 0{,}45\) the bar rotates from \(\theta_0\) by \(0{,}008185\) rad, at the doubled \(p = 0{,}9\) by \(0{,}095491\) rad, that is \(11{,}7\) times more, not twice. There is no superposition. The linear model writes equilibrium on the initial position, so its graph is the straight line with the slope of the curve at \(p = 0\). Its rotation is \(p\,s_0/\cos^2\theta_0\), so at \(p = 0{,}9\) it is \(0{,}0090\) rad, more than ten times too little. That is the modelling error as a number. Beyond the top \(0{,}931\) the curve turns down (the dashed part), and we shall meet this top as the limit load. At \(p = 0{,}9\) the equation \(g = 0\) has three solutions in \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\), namely \(\theta = -0{,}4921\), \(0{,}1055\) and \(0{,}3919\) rad. The last two are the intersections of the horizontal line \(p = 0{,}9\) with the curve, the full dot on the rising part and the hollow one on the falling part, the first is at a negative angle outside the figure. Which is the real position of the bar? The answer is in theorem 8.71. The second derivatives \(V''/(kL^2)\) are \(-0{,}2444\), \(+0{,}0839\) and \(-0{,}1197\), so only the middle one, the full dot, is stable (definition 8.72). These are three of the properties that COOK (PDF p. 610) lists for nonlinear equations: superposition does not hold, each load case needs its own analysis and for a given load there can be more than one solution. The fourth, that reversing the order of loading can change the result, stays with COOK.

COOK (PDF pp. 609 and 610) distinguishes three kinds of nonlinearity. In material nonlinearity the material properties are functions of stress or strain (plasticity, creep), so the graph of force against displacement bends and its slope is smaller at larger displacement. In contact nonlinearity a gap opens or closes: while the gap is open there is no force, once it closes the slope jumps. Geometric nonlinearity is the one of the previous section, where equilibrium is written on the tilted position and the slope changes with the position. In all three the stiffness matrix, sometimes the right-hand side too, becomes a function of the displacements: \(\mat K(\vek D)\,\vek D = \vek R\). We cannot compute the displacements directly, because \(\mat K\) needs the displacements. This section treats only geometric nonlinearity on models with one unknown. Material and contact nonlinearity are named, not treated (for contact see chapter 25, plasticity is not in the book). A limit of models with one unknown is that they do not show how Newton's method deals with a matrix of size one thousand.

17.7.2 Tangent stiffness and Newton's method

For a nonlinear equation \(g(\theta) = 0\) we cannot find the root in one step, but we can solve a linear equation. The idea is the same as for the derivative: at a point we know, we replace the curve by its tangent and find the zero of the tangent. So we first name the slope.

Definition 17.31 Tangent stiffness (tangentna togost)

Let a system have \(n\) generalized coordinates \(\vek q\) in an open set \(D \subset \mathbb R^n\) and a twice continuously differentiable potential energy \(V\) (definition 8.58). The imbalance column \(\vek g(\vek q)\) of \(n\) numbers has components \(g_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial V/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\), so \(\vek g = -\vek Q\). By corollary 8.63 the point \(\vek q\) is an equilibrium exactly when \(\vek g(\vek q) = \vek 0\). The tangent stiffness at \(\vek q\) is the \(n \times n\) matrix (for one coordinate the slope of the tangent to the graph of the imbalance)

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}(\vek q) = \frac{\partial\vek g}{\partial\vek q}(\vek q) , \qquad (\mat K_{\mathrm{t}})_{\mathrm{sr}} = \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial q_{\mathrm{r}}} , \tag{17.28}\]

the Hessian matrix of the energy (definition 8.69). For one coordinate it is the number \(V''(q)\). If \(\vek q^\ast\) is an equilibrium, positive definiteness of \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}(\vek q^\ast)\) tells by theorem 8.71 that the equilibrium is energetically stable.

Source: COOK (PDF p. 610) for one unknown: \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = \mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}u\), the slope of the graph of force against displacement. The definition with the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is ours.

The name is so because \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is the slope of the tangent to the graph of the imbalance. For a linear structure with the energy \(\tfrac12\vek q^\T\mat K\vek q - \vek R^\T\vek q\) we have \(\vek g = \mat K\vek q - \vek R\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}} = \mat K\), the constant stiffness matrix of chapters 7 and 12. For a nonlinear one \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is different at every position. For our model (ii), differentiating the right-hand side of (17.27) by the product rule,

\[\frac{K_{\mathrm{t}}}{kL^2} = \frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta} = \cos^2\theta - (\sin\theta - s_0)\sin\theta - p\cos\theta . \tag{17.29}\]

At the straight perfect position (\(\theta = 0\), \(s_0 = 0\)), that is on the vertical blackwhite branch of figure 17.54, we have \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = 1 - p\). The one is the elastic part of the spring and the term \(-p\) is the part that the compressive load takes away, as in equation (12.56), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} + \mu\,\mat G_{\mathrm{ff}}\). The zero is at \(p = 1\), so the critical load of the perfect model (ii) is \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = kL\). For model (i) it is \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = k_{\mathrm{r}}/L\) by example 8.74.

Definition 17.32 Newton's method (Newtonova metoda)

Let \(\vek g\colon D \to \mathbb R^n\) be the imbalance of definition 17.31 at a given load and \(\vek q^{(0)} \in D\) a starting estimate. Step \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) is: solve the linear system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}(\vek q^{(k)})\,\Delta\vek q = -\vek g(\vek q^{(k)})\) and put \(\vek q^{(k+1)} = \vek q^{(k)} + \Delta\vek q\). We stop when the imbalance is small enough (the measure is in the text below). For one unknown, \(\theta^{(k+1)} = \theta^{(k)} - g(\theta^{(k)})/g'(\theta^{(k)})\), the zero of the tangent at the point \(\theta^{(k)}\).

Source: COOK (PDF p. 611) says that the method is called Newton's method in calculus texts and Newton-Raphson (N-R) in structural mechanics, and describes it as a way of generating the curve of load against displacement. The notation is ours.

The name is Newton's, as COOK (PDF p. 611) says, why the name Raphson is added in structural mechanics the source does not say. Figure 17.57 shows the method on model (ii) at \(p = 0{,}9\). On the left panel the horizontal is the angle \(\theta\), the vertical the imbalance \(g\) (heights are enlarged 250 times in the figure). The blue curve is the graph of \(g(\theta; 0{,}9)\). We start at the point \(\theta^{(0)} = \theta_0 = 0{,}01\), where \(g = -0{,}009\). Through this point we draw the tangent with the slope \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) and find where it crosses the axis: that is \(\theta^{(1)} = 0{,}100048\). The next tangent is already so near the curve that we cannot tell them apart in the figure. The remaining iterates are \(0{,}1054390\) and \(0{,}1054914\), and the root is \(\theta^\ast = 0{,}10549145\).

Does this procedure always converge, and how fast? The answer shows on one step, drawn in figure 17.58. Its curve is bent more than the column's so that we can see it, \(g = 0{,}4\,\theta^2 + 0{,}6\,\theta - 1\) with the root \(1\).

On the axes \(\theta\) runs across and \(g\) up. The blackwhite curve is the graph of \(g\), the root \(\theta^\ast\) is where it crosses the axis. We stand at the point \(\theta^{(k)}\), the error \(e_{\mathrm{k}}\) is its distance to the root. The tangent at this point crosses the axis at the new iterate \(\theta^{(k+1)}\), which is still \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) away from the root. If \(g\) were a straight line, the tangent would lie on it and the step would hit the root. It misses only by as much as the curve moves away from the tangent on the way from \(\theta^{(k)}\) to \(\theta^\ast\): above the root the tangent is \(\tfrac12 g''(c)\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) below the curve. The gap grows with the square of the distance, because the tangent captures the value and the slope but not the curvature. From the bottom of this gap the tangent climbs with the slope \(g'(\theta^{(k)})\) to the axis exactly over the distance \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), so \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) is the gap divided by the slope. In the numbers of the figure \(e_{\mathrm{k}} = 2\), \(g'' = 0{,}8\) and \(g'(\theta^{(k)}) = 3\), the gap is \(\tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}8 \cdot 2^2 = 1{,}6\) and \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1} = 1{,}6/3 = 0{,}533\). The theorem says this precisely for one unknown. In it we use Taylor's theorem with the second derivative (theorem 8.68), the only tool of this kind in this section. Its two hypotheses can be read off the figure: the slope of the tangent must not be zero, or the tangent does not cross the axis, and the gap divided by the slope must be smaller than the error itself, or the step does not come closer.

Theorem 17.33 Quadratic convergence of Newton's method (kvadratična konvergenca Newtonove metode)

Let \(g\) be a twice continuously differentiable function of one variable on the closed interval \(I = [\theta^\ast - r, \theta^\ast + r]\) with \(g(\theta^\ast) = 0\). Let \(m > 0\) and \(M\) be numbers with \(|g'(\theta)| \ge m\) and \(|g''(\theta)| \le M\) for every \(\theta \in I\). Let \(K = M/(2m)\). If the starting estimate \(\theta^{(0)} \in I\) and \(K\,|\theta^{(0)} - \theta^\ast| < 1\), all iterates \(\theta^{(k)}\) of Newton's method lie in \(I\) and the error \(e_{\mathrm{k}} = \theta^{(k)} - \theta^\ast\) before a step and the error \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) after it satisfy

\[|e_{\mathrm{k}+1}| \le K\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2 , \qquad K\,|e_{\mathrm{k}}| \le \big(K\,|e_0|\big)^{2^k} . \tag{17.30}\]
Proof

We must show the one-step error estimate and then, by induction, that the iterates stay in \(I\) and the error falls.

  1. Let \(\theta^{(k)} \in I\) and \(e_{\mathrm{k}} \ne 0\). By theorem 8.68 with \(x_0 = \theta^{(k)}\) and \(x = \theta^\ast\) there is a point \(c\) between them, hence in \(I\), with \(0 = g(\theta^\ast) = g(\theta^{(k)}) - g'(\theta^{(k)})\,e_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12 g''(c)\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). The first two terms are the height of the tangent above the root, the third is the gap between the curve and it.
  2. Since \(|g'(\theta^{(k)})| \ge m > 0\) we may divide by \(g'(\theta^{(k)})\): \(0 = g(\theta^{(k)})/g'(\theta^{(k)}) - e_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12\,g''(c)/g'(\theta^{(k)})\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). By definition 17.32, \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1} = e_{\mathrm{k}} - g(\theta^{(k)})/g'(\theta^{(k)})\). So \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \tfrac12\,g''(c)/g'(\theta^{(k)})\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\): the new error is the gap divided by the slope of the tangent, which is not horizontal because \(m > 0\).
  3. The bound \(|g''| \le M\) limits the gap from above and the bound \(|g'| \ge m\) the slope of the tangent from below, so it follows that \(|e_{\mathrm{k}+1}| \le K\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). If \(e_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\), then \(\theta^{(k)}\) is a root and the estimate holds.
  4. Let \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}} = K|e_{\mathrm{k}}|\). Step 3 gives \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}+1} \le \delta_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). Since \(\delta_0 < 1\), induction gives \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}} \le \delta_0^{2^k}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}} < 1\) for every \(k\).
  5. From \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}} < 1\) it follows that \(|e_{\mathrm{k}+1}| \le K\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2 = \delta_{\mathrm{k}}\,|e_{\mathrm{k}}| < |e_{\mathrm{k}}| \le r\), so \(\theta^{(k+1)} \in I\) and step 1 holds for every \(k\). In the figure \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) is shorter than \(e_{\mathrm{k}}\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK (PDF p. 612) says that the errors of Newton's method usually fall, and adds that convergence is not guaranteed for every nonlinear problem.

The theorem says that the number of correct decimals roughly doubles after each step. We check it on figure 17.57, left. The errors of the iterates against the root at \(p = 0{,}9\) are \(e_0 = 9{,}55\cdot 10^{-2}\), \(5{,}44\cdot 10^{-3}\), \(5{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\) and \(5{,}16\cdot 10^{-9}\) and the ratios \(|e_{\mathrm{k}+1}|/e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) are \(0{,}60\), \(1{,}77\) and \(1{,}87\). By step 2 the ratio must tend to \(|g''(\theta^\ast)|/(2\,g'(\theta^\ast)) = 0{,}3141/(2\cdot 0{,}08388) = 1{,}87\) (the numbers \(g''\) and \(g'\) are from NumPy at the root), and it does. We did not compute the constants \(m\) and \(M\) for the whole interval \(I\). The theorem guarantees convergence, here we observe it in the ratios.

Example 17.34 Where the theorem fails: zero stiffness and the wrong root (kje izrek ne velja: ničelna togost in napačen koren)

Theorem 17.33 has two hypotheses that a column can lose: \(|g'| \ge m > 0\) on the interval \(I\) (the tangent is not horizontal) and a starting estimate close to the root (\(K\,|e_0| < 1\), the start near the root). For each we show a case where it is missing.

The first is \(m = 0\), that is \(g'(\theta^\ast) = 0\). For \(g(x) = x^2\) the root is \(0\) and \(g' = 2x\), so \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - x_{\mathrm{k}}^2/(2x_{\mathrm{k}}) = x_{\mathrm{k}}/2\), the iterates are \(1\), \(0{,}5\), \(0{,}25\), \(0{,}125\). The error only halves at each step, the convergence is linear. In our model the stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero at the limit load: the curve of the left panel would, at \(p = 0{,}93119\), only touch the axis and the tangent at the root would be horizontal. As we approach the limit load \(0{,}93119\) at \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\), Newton's method needs more and more iterations: at \(p = 0{,}9\), \(0{,}92\), \(0{,}93\) and \(0{,}931\) these are \(4\), \(5\), \(6\) and \(7\) iterations for an imbalance below \(10^{-13}\), and the stiffness at the root is \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = 0{,}0839\), \(0{,}0506\), \(0{,}0173\) and \(0{,}0071\).

The second is a start far from the root, and with it the root that the method finds. At \(p = 0{,}95\), above the limit load, the right panel of figure 17.57 shows that the graph of \(g\) does not cross the axis on the right side. From the start \(\theta^{(0)} = 0{,}01\) the iterates along the tangents are \(0{,}2002\), \(-0{,}2708\), \(-0{,}4877\), \(-0{,}4087\), \(-0{,}3895\) and after eight steps \(-0{,}388299\). The hypothesis of the theorem is missing here: \(g'(0{,}01) = 0{,}050 > 0\) while \(g' < 0\) at the root, so \(g'\) has a zero between the start and the root and there is no interval \(I\) with \(m > 0\) that holds both. At the end, when the iterates are near the root, the convergence is quadratic, as the theorem promises. But the root is an equilibrium with \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = -0{,}16976 < 0\), which by theorem 8.71 (part 2) is not energetically stable. At \(p = 0{,}95\) it is the only equilibrium in \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\) (NumPy). So the convergence of Newton's method says nothing about stability, it only guarantees that the imbalance is zero. If we start from the last solution at \(p = 0{,}9\) instead of from \(\theta_0\), the first seven iterates jump between \(0{,}13\) and \(0{,}36\) rad, then the method leaps away and after \(15\) steps stops at \(\theta = -9{,}43\) rad. This is a root of the equation because of the periodicity of the sine, not a position of the bar we modelled.

Newton's method needs the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) and a solution of a system at every step. For a large system this is the most expensive part (the factorization of lemma 7.47, the cost by section 17.6). The modified Newton-Raphson method (spremenjena Newtonova metoda) uses the same \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\), computed at the starting position, in all steps, that is the slope of the first tangent at all later points too, so it computes the factorization once (COOK, PDF p. 612). On our example (\(p = 0{,}9\)) it needs \(15\) iterations instead of \(4\) to reach an imbalance below \(10^{-14}\) and the error falls at each step only to \(0{,}16\) of the previous one, which is linear convergence. The saving is in the cost of a step, not in the number of steps.

How do we choose the starting estimate and when do we stop? COOK (PDF p. 612) recommends applying the load in steps and starting each time from the solution of the previous one. Each solution is one point of the path in figure 17.55. At \(p = 0{,}3\), \(0{,}6\) and \(0{,}9\), starting from the previous solution, we get \(\theta = 0{,}014287\), \(0{,}025014\) and \(0{,}105491\) rad with \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\) iterations, and one step to \(p = 0{,}9\) needs \(4\) too. For such mild nonlinearity there is no saving, not even just below the limit load: at \(p = 0{,}931\) one step from \(\theta_0\) finds the stable position \(0{,}20592\) rad in \(7\) iterations, and a step from the solution at \(p = 0{,}93\) finds the same position in \(5\). The steps pay off in another way. Each gives one point of the path, as COOK (PDF p. 611) describes the method, and when the load exceeds the limit load, the iteration from the last solution no longer finds a nearby equilibrium and jumps far away, as in example 17.34. We stop when the imbalance is a small share of the load and the step a small share of the initial step (COOK, PDF pp. 615 and 616, tolerances between \(0{,}001\) and \(0{,}01\)). We denote the tolerance by \(\delta\). Here the measure is \(|g| \le \delta\,p\), since \(P L = p\,kL^2\) is the moment that the load contributes. With \(\delta = 10^{-3}\) and \(p = 0{,}9\) the method stops already after the first step: \(|g| = 4{,}6\cdot 10^{-4} < 9\cdot 10^{-4}\). But \(\theta^{(1)}\) has an error of \(5{,}4\cdot 10^{-3}\) rad, which is \(5{,}2\) % of \(\theta^\ast\), since the error is about \(g/K_{\mathrm{t}} = 4{,}6\cdot 10^{-4}/0{,}0839\). A small imbalance with a small stiffness means a large displacement error. COOK (PDF p. 616) warns that the displacement criterion alone is not sufficient and should be supplemented by the force criterion. Our example shows the opposite side: the force criterion alone is too lenient at small stiffness. So we use both. When we reach \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) we have a limit point and the method fails, as example 17.34 shows. COOK (PDF p. 613) describes the arc-length method (metoda dolžine loka), which changes the load during the iterations so that the points lie on a circle around the starting point, and can pass a limit point. We only name it, we do not compute it.

17.7.3 Imperfections and the limit load

What do the two models say about a column? The load that linear buckling analysis predicts for a column is, by definition 12.51, the first \(\mu\) at which \(\mat K + \mu\,\mat G\) is singular. For both models this is the same: the stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) at \(\theta = 0\) is zero at \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), for (i) at \(k_{\mathrm{r}}/L\), for (ii) at \(kL\). Linear analysis reads only the zero of \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) and does not tell apart two models that do not differ in it. They differ in where the bar goes when \(P\) exceeds \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), and the lower part of figure 17.54 shows it, with the angle \(\theta\) across and \(P/P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) up on its axes and the paths of the two perfect models.
