The perfect model (i) has, by example 8.74, the bent branch \(P/P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \theta/\sin\theta \ge 1\), which rises and is stable: a column that bends still carries more load. The same holds for the continuous perfect column: by theorem 8.148 \(P/P_{\mathrm{cr}} = (2K(k)/\pi)^2\), and at the tip angle \(\alpha = 0{,}5\), \(1{,}0\) and \(\pi/2\) rad this is \(1{,}032\), \(1{,}137\) and \(1{,}393\) (NumPy, \(K\) by the arithmetic-geometric mean). In the perfect model (ii) the opposite happens. At \(s_0 = 0\) we have \(g = \sin\theta\,(\cos\theta - p)\), so equilibrium \(\theta = 0\) and the branch \(p = \cos\theta\), which falls. By equation (17.29) on this branch \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta = -\sin^2\theta < 0\), so it is not stable by theorem 8.71 (part 2). The energy at the critical point shows it too. At \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) the energy of the perfect model (i) is \(V - V(0) = k_{\mathrm{r}}\,(\theta^2/2 - 1 + \cos\theta) > 0\) for \(\theta \ne 0\) (equation (8.72)), and for (ii), with \(\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta\),

\[V(\theta) - V(0) = kL^2\big(\tfrac12\sin^2\theta + \cos\theta - 1\big) = -\tfrac12\,kL^2\,(1 - \cos\theta)^2 < 0 . \tag{17.31}\]

The straight position of model (ii) at the critical load is not energetically stable (definition 8.72), since every other position has lower energy. At \(\theta = 0{,}1\) and \(0{,}5\) rad the difference is \(-1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\,kL^2\) and \(-7{,}49\cdot 10^{-3}\,kL^2\), and for (i) it is \(+4{,}2\cdot 10^{-6}\,k_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(+2{,}6\cdot 10^{-3}\,k_{\mathrm{r}}\). The same \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), the opposite decision: this is why linear buckling analysis must stay a first step, not a verdict.

A perfect column cannot be reached, so the imperfect one interests us. For model (i) the outcome of example 8.74 is mild: all equilibria on the path from the unloaded position \(\theta_0\) are stable, the path rises smoothly, there is no limit load (thin blue curve). For model (ii) an equilibrium with \(\theta > \theta_0\) at load \(p\) is a solution of \(p = f(\theta)\), where

\[f(\theta) = \Big(1 - \frac{s_0}{\sin\theta}\Big)\cos\theta . \tag{17.32}\]

This expression is the same as \(g = 0\), since \(g = \sin\theta\,\big(f(\theta) - p\big)\). The orange curves in the figure are \(p = f(\theta)\) for three imperfections. The function \(f\) is zero at \(\theta_0\) and \(\pi/2\) and positive between, so it has a largest value on \([\theta_0, \pi/2]\) (the maximum theorem, 8.27 for one variable). We call this value the limit load (mejna sila), because it is the bound of the load above which there is no equilibrium with \(\theta\) near \(\theta_0\) (example 8.75, limit point). The word bound matters here: from this load on, a bar loaded gradually cannot stay near its previous position and moves far away, as in the snap-through (preskok) of example 8.75.

How large is the limit load and where does it come from? Near the top \(\cos\theta \approx 1 - s^2/2\) with \(s = \sin\theta\), so \(f \approx 1 - s_0/s - s^2/2\): two pieces are taken off the full critical load. Panel (a) of figure 17.59 draws them for \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad.

On the axes of panel (a) \(s\) runs across and the loss \(1 - p\) up. The first piece \(s_0/s\) is the price of the imperfection: the spring feels only the part \(s - s_0\) of the offset \(s\), which is the share \(1 - s_0/s\), and this piece falls as \(s\) grows. The second piece \(s^2/2\) is the price of leaning, which the perfect column pays too on its branch \(p = \cos\theta\), and it grows. Their sum therefore has a bottom, and the limit load is one minus this bottom. The bottom is where the first piece falls as fast as the second grows: \(s_0/s^2 = s\), so at \(s = s_0^{1/3} = 0{,}215\). There the first piece \(s_0/s = s^2\) is exactly twice the second, so the sum is made of three equal parts of \(0{,}0232\), together \(0{,}0696 = \tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3}\). This is where the exponent \(2/3\) comes from: the piece \(s^2/2\) at \(s = s_0^{1/3}\) equals \(\tfrac12 s_0^{2/3}\). Panel (b) magnifies the top of the curve \(f\) on the axes \(s\) and \(p\). The largest value \(0{,}93119\) lies between the lower bound \(0{,}93038\) and the upper bound \(0{,}93538\), which are \(\tfrac12 s_0 = 0{,}0050\) apart. The computation above is approximate, since we replaced \(\cos\theta\) by \(1 - s^2/2\). The theorem proves the two bounds without the approximation and for every \(\theta_0\).

Theorem 17.35 Limit load of the imperfect column (mejna sila nepopolnega stebra)

Let model (ii) have the imperfection \(\theta_0 \in (0, \pi/2)\), \(s_0 = \sin\theta_0\), and let \(f\) be the function of equation (17.32) on \([\theta_0, \pi/2]\). Let \(p_\mathrm{lim}\) be its largest value, the limit load \(P_\mathrm{lim} = p_\mathrm{lim}\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). Then:

  1. At an equilibrium \(p = f(\theta)\) with \(\theta \in (\theta_0, \pi/2)\) we have \(V''(\theta) = kL^2\sin\theta\,f'(\theta)\). The equilibrium is energetically stable if \(f'(\theta) > 0\) (the rising part of the path) and is not if \(f'(\theta) < 0\) (the falling part).
  2. For \(p > p_\mathrm{lim}\), above the peak of the curve \(f\), there is no equilibrium in \((\theta_0, \pi/2)\).
  3. \(1 - \tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3} \le p_\mathrm{lim} \le 1 - \tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3} + \tfrac12\,s_0\) (the lower and upper bound).
Proof

We must show the second derivative at equilibrium, then an upper and a lower bound of the largest value by two estimates of \(\cos\theta\).

  1. For \(\theta \in (\theta_0, \pi/2)\) we have \(\sin\theta > 0\) and \(V'(\theta) = kL^2\sin\theta\,\big(f(\theta) - p\big)\). By the product rule \(V'' = kL^2\cos\theta\,(f - p) + kL^2\sin\theta\,f'\), the first term is zero at equilibrium. The rest follows from theorem 8.71 (part 1 for \(f' > 0\), part 2 for \(f' < 0\), since \(\sin\theta > 0\)). In figure 17.55 these are the rising, solid part of the path and the falling, dashed one.
  2. Since \(p_\mathrm{lim}\) is the largest value of \(f\), for \(p > p_\mathrm{lim}\) the equation \(f(\theta) = p\) has no solution: a horizontal line above the top does not cross the curve \(f\).
  3. For \(x \in [0, 1]\) we have \(\sqrt{1 - x} \le 1 - x/2\), because after squaring \(1 - x \le 1 - x + x^2/4\). Also \(\sqrt{1 - x} \ge (1 - x)(1 + x/2) = 1 - x/2 - x^2/2\), which for \(x = 1\) holds as \(0 = 0\), and for \(x < 1\), after dividing by \(\sqrt{1 - x} > 0\), is \(1 \ge \sqrt{1 - x}\,(1 + x/2)\), after squaring \(1 \ge (1 - x)(1 + x + x^2/4) = 1 - \tfrac34 x^2 - \tfrac14 x^3\), which holds. With \(x = s^2\), \(s = \sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - s^2}\) for \(\theta \in [0, \pi/2]\) we get \(1 - s^2/2 - s^4/2 \le \cos\theta \le 1 - s^2/2\).
  4. Upper bound. Since \(1 - s_0/s \ge 0\) for \(s \ge s_0\), by step 3 \(f \le (1 - s_0/s)(1 - s^2/2) = 1 - s_0/s - s^2/2 + s_0 s/2 \le 1 - (s_0/s + s^2/2) + s_0/2\), because \(s \le 1\). In the bracket is the sum of the two pieces of figure 17.59.
  5. The inequality of the arithmetic and geometric means for three positive numbers, \(a_1 + a_2 + a_3 \ge 3\,(a_1 a_2 a_3)^{1/3}\), with \(a_1 = a_2 = s_0/(2s)\) and \(a_3 = s^2/2\), gives \(s_0/s + s^2/2 \ge 3\,(s_0^2/8)^{1/3} = \tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3}\). This is the bottom of the sum, where the three parts are equal. Hence \(f \le 1 - \tfrac32 s_0^{2/3} + \tfrac12 s_0\) and so is \(p_\mathrm{lim}\), which is the upper bound.
  6. Lower bound. Let \(s_1 = s_0^{1/3}\) and \(a = s_0^{2/3} = s_1^2\). Since \(s_0 < 1\), we have \(s_0 < s_1 < 1\), so \(\theta_1 = \arcsin s_1\) lies in \((\theta_0, \pi/2)\). By step 3, \(\cos\theta_1 \ge 1 - a/2 - a^2/2\) and \(1 - s_0/s_1 = 1 - a \ge 0\), so \(f(\theta_1) \ge (1 - a)(1 - a/2 - a^2/2) = 1 - \tfrac32 a + \tfrac12 a^3 \ge 1 - \tfrac32 a\). Since \(p_\mathrm{lim} \ge f(\theta_1)\), the lower bound is proved: the point of the curve at \(s_1\) lies above it.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK (PDF p. 668) calls a structure whose limit load is strongly affected by small changes of geometry, load or support imperfection-sensitive and gives no formula for the law. The name of the author of this phenomenon is not on that page, so we name it after no one.

The theorem says that the loss \(1 - p_\mathrm{lim}\) equals \(\tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3}\) to within \(\tfrac12 s_0\), it is not proportional to \(s_0\): for small \(s_0\), \(s_0^{2/3}\) is much larger than \(s_0\) (at \(s_0 = 0{,}01\), \(s_0^{2/3} = 0{,}046\)). For this model even more holds. The derivative of \(f\) with respect to \(s\) is zero exactly at \(s^3 = s_0\) (SymPy: \(f'(s)\,s^2\sqrt{1 - s^2} = s_0 - s^3\)), so the top is exactly at \(s_1 = s_0^{1/3}\) and \(p_\mathrm{lim} = (1 - s_0^{2/3})^{3/2}\). The bounds of the theorem are the beginning of this expression, \(1 - \tfrac32 s_0^{2/3}\), with a band of width \(\tfrac12 s_0\) for the remainder. In the table the limit loads are the dots on the orange curves of figure 17.54. Numbers from NumPy, which checks the theorem (largest value over a grid of \(2\cdot 10^6\) points):

\(\theta_0\) (rad) 0,001 0,01 0,05
\(p_\mathrm{lim}\) 0,98504 0,93119 0,80354
at the angle \(\theta\) (rad) 0,1002 0,2171 0,3772
lower bound 0,98500 0,93038 0,79648
upper bound 0,98550 0,93538 0,82146
loss \(1 - p_\mathrm{lim}\) 1,50 % 6,88 % 19,65 %

With \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad, that is 10 mm on 1 m, the column carries only \(0{,}931\) of the critical load, with \(\theta_0 = 0{,}05\) rad, 50 mm per metre, only \(0{,}804\). A tenfold smaller imperfection gives how much smaller a loss? The law says \(10^{2/3} = 4{,}64\): a tenfold smaller imperfection (\(0{,}001\) instead of \(0{,}01\) rad) reduces the loss from \(6{,}9\) % only to \(1{,}5\) %, not to a tenth. The largest error within the bounds of the theorem (the unknown term up to \(s_0/2\)) at \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad is \(0{,}005\), which is \(7\) % of the loss \(6{,}9\) %. The bounds in the table lie below and above the computed value.

Do real columns lose this much? COOK (PDF p. 668) states that the limit load of real thin shells may be only about \(10\) % of the load of linear buckling analysis, and about \(50\) % in the laboratory with great effort. For a plane frame of bars with a cross section of 8 mm × 8 mm (\(E = 200\) GPa) COOK (PDF pp. 669 and 670) gives linear buckling at \(137\) N, and the perfect nonlinear analysis shows that the frame does not buckle at all. When node \(D\) is moved 2 mm sideways, linear buckling is at \(114\) N and the nonlinear analysis gives snap-through at \(86\) N, which is \(0{,}754\) of the load of linear analysis. Our model (ii) with the imperfection \(2/480 = 0{,}0042\) gives by the law \(1{,}5\,s_0^{2/3}\) a loss of \(3{,}9\) %, the frame loses \(25\) % (against the \(137\) N of the perfect frame, \(37\) %). The difference is not surprising: the frame is not one rigid bar with one spring. The model shows the mechanism and the form of the law, not the number of this frame. It also shows what COOK (PDF p. 668) says about models: the imperfection must be introduced deliberately, because small numerical errors do not steer the computation into an imperfect mode. In our perfect model (ii) with \(p = 1{,}1\) and the start at \(\theta = 0\) we have exactly \(g(0) = 0\), and Newton's method stays at \(\theta = 0\): the straight position on the dashed part of the vertical branch, where \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = -0{,}100 < 0\) and which is not stable. The imperfection we introduce can be the buckling mode of linear buckling analysis (COOK, PDF p. 668), so linear analysis stays a useful first step.

What does the theorem cover and what not? It is proved for model (ii). That the same law holds for every column with an unstable perfect path the section does not prove, COOK (PDF pp. 668 and 669) shows the phenomenon on shells and on a frame with numbers. For the continuous column, theorem 8.148, theorem 8.147 and theorem 12.53 are about the perfect column, an imperfect continuous column needs its own model.

17.7.4 Summary of the section

A nonlinear model has the imbalance \(\vek g(\vek q) = \vek 0\) and the tangent stiffness \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}(\vek q)\) of definition 17.31. Newton's method (definition 17.32) solves \(\vek g = \vek 0\) with tangents. By theorem 17.33 the convergence is quadratic if \(K_{\mathrm{t}} \ne 0\) at the root and the starting estimate is close enough to the root. Example 17.34 showed that at \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) it becomes linear and that convergence says nothing about the stability of the equilibrium found. Linear buckling analysis gives the same critical load for two columns that only the energy and the imperfection tell apart. In model (ii) the limit load with imperfection \(\theta_0\) is lower by about \(\tfrac32\,\sin^{2/3}\theta_0\) (theorem 17.35, the top of the path). The three errors: the modelling error is that the linear model knows nothing of the limit load, the numerical error is the stopped iteration (\(5{,}2\) % at a premature stop), there is no discretization error. Nonlinear dynamics follows in the next section.

17.8 Nonlinear dynamics and numerical damping

A pendulum of length \(l = 1\) m is released from the position in which the rod is horizontal. For small deflections the period would be \(2\pi\sqrt{l/g} = 2{,}006\) s, but at a deflection of \(90°\) it is \(2{,}368\) s by theorem 8.139, which is \(18\) % longer. The linear model does not suffice here, because the force on the pendulum is not a linear function of the deflection. In section 17.7 we solved such equations in statics with Newton's method. Now the question is about time: how do we step the equation of motion when the force is nonlinear, and how do we prevent the scheme of chapter 10 from exciting oscillations in the mesh that the model does not have at all? The exact swing from \(90°\) is the grey curve further down in this section.

After section 17.1 (definition 17.2) this section treats the other two kinds of error: the error of discretizing time with a step \(\Delta t\) and the numerical error of the stopped iterations of Newton's method. The modelling error is not reduced: the pendulum is a model of a rigid rod and a point mass, without friction in the pivot and without air. Reducing the step does not reduce the mesh error of section 17.3 either, because the two errors add.

17.8.1 The Newmark family (Newmarkova družina)

In chapter 10 we met two schemes. The trapezoidal rule (definition 10.92) is implicit and unconditionally stable without damping. Central differences (definition 10.97) are explicit and stable only below the critical step. We write both with the same idea: the velocity and the displacement at the end of the step are known from the start of the step and from the acceleration, and the acceleration is fixed by the equation of motion at the end of the step. They differ in how the acceleration is averaged over the step. The velocity changes over a step by \(\Delta t\) times the mean acceleration, so we replace it by the weighted sum \((1 - \gamma)\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \gamma\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) with two weights that add to \(1\). For the displacement we take, for each component, the expansion with a Taylor remainder (theorem 8.68): \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = q_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12\Delta t^2\,a(\xi)\) with a point \(\xi\) in the step that may differ from component to component. We replace the term \(\tfrac12 a(\xi)\) by a weighted sum of \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) with the weights \(\tfrac12 - \beta\) and \(\beta\), which add to \(\tfrac12\). Two numbers, \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\), are therefore free, and each pair gives its own scheme. That is why we call it a family. It is named after N. M. Newmark, who proposed it (COOK §11.13, PDF p. 432, BATHE §9.2.3, PDF p. 794). In this section the letters \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) mean only these two parameters, not the shear strain of chapter 1 or anything else. Figure 17.60 shows both weighted sums: the mean acceleration for the velocity and the gap in displacement for the displacement.

Definition 17.36 Newmark family (Newmarkova družina)

Let \(\mat M\) be a positive definite and \(\mat C\) and \(\mat K\) symmetric matrices of order \(n\), \(\vek Q(t)\) a column of forces, \(\Delta t > 0\) a step, \(\vek q_0\) and \(\vek v_0\) the initial columns, and \(\gamma\) and \(\beta \ge 0\) real numbers. The Newmark scheme with parameters \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) is the sequence of columns \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\) determined by the initial columns, by equation (10.117) at \(k = 0\) (which gives \(\vek a_0\)) and, for every \(k \ge 0\), by the two equations, which average the acceleration and the displacement

\[\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t^2\Big(\big(\tfrac12 - \beta\big)\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \beta\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\Big) , \tag{17.33}\]
\[\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,\Big((1 - \gamma)\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \gamma\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\Big) , \tag{17.34}\]

together with equation (10.117) at \(k + 1\). At \(\beta = 0\) the scheme is explicit (equation (17.33) does not contain \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\)), at \(\beta > 0\) it is implicit.

Source: COOK (11.13-3), PDF p. 432, with parameters \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\). BATHE (9.18) and (9.19), PDF p. 794, with parameters \(\delta = \gamma\) and \(\alpha = \beta\). The reason with weights above is ours.

Figure 17.60 shows one step from \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\) to \(t_{\mathrm{k}+1} = t_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\) in one coordinate. At the top we draw the acceleration, running from \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) to \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). Between the two stands the weighted sum: from \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) we take the share \(1 - \gamma\), from \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) the share \(\gamma\), and we get the mean acceleration, the height of the horizontal line. The rectangle under the line has the area \(\Delta t\) times the mean acceleration, which is the increase of velocity in equation (17.34). At the bottom we draw the displacement. Without acceleration it would be carried by the tangent with velocity \(v_{\mathrm{k}}\), the acceleration bends it, and the gap at the end of the step is \(\Delta t^2\) times the weighted sum \((\tfrac12 - \beta)\,a_{\mathrm{k}} + \beta\,a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), as in equation (17.33).

Both schemes of chapter 10 are in the family.

Lemma 17.37 The trapezoidal rule and central differences in the Newmark family (Trapezno pravilo in centralne diference v Newmarkovi družini)
  1. At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) and \(\beta = \tfrac14\) the Newmark scheme is the trapezoidal rule of definition 10.92. In figure 17.61 this is the filled circle.
  2. At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = 0\) and \(\mat C = \mat 0\) the sequence \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) satisfies equation (10.126) at \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) and coincides with the central differences of definition 10.97. In figure 17.61 this is the empty circle at \(\beta = 0\).
Proof

We show that equations (17.33) and (17.34) turn into the equations of chapter 10.

  1. At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) equation (17.34) is equation (10.119). At \(\beta = \tfrac14\) the right side of equation (17.33) equals \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1})\). From equation (10.119) we have \(\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1})\), so this is \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1})\), which is equation (10.118). This is point 1. This equality describes the trapezoidal rule in the parameter plane.
  2. At \(\beta = 0\) we have \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{2}\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\). We insert equation (17.34) with \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) into the same expression for step \(k + 1\): \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+2} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{2}\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{2}(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}) + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{2}\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). This is how the point \(\beta = 0\) of the parameter plane behaves.
  3. We subtract the first equality from the second: \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+2} - 2\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \Delta t^2\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). Since \(\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = -\mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) at \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) and \(\mat C = \mat 0\), this is equation (10.126) at index \(k + 1\). The start \(\vek q_1 = \vek q_0 + \Delta t\,\vek v_0 + \tfrac12\Delta t^2\vek a_0\) is the start of definition 10.97. This is point 2. This is the same point of the parameter plane.

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 432): "average acceleration" is \(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = \tfrac14\). BATHE §9.2.3 (PDF p. 794): the same as the "constant-average-acceleration method (also called trapezoidal rule)". The sources do not state point 2 in this form. The proof is not from a source.

Figure 17.61 shows the family in the plane of the parameters. We draw a horizontal axis \(\gamma\) and a vertical axis \(\beta\). Both parameters lie on them, and every point of the plane is one scheme. The first point is the trapezoidal rule at \(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = \tfrac14\), which lemma 17.37 places in the family. Below it on the same vertical are \(\beta = \tfrac16\), the linear acceleration scheme that COOK and BATHE name (COOK PDF p. 432, BATHE PDF p. 794), and \(\beta = 0\), central differences by point 2 of the lemma. Both are only conditionally stable (COOK (11.13-8), PDF p. 433), and for central differences theorem 10.99 proves it. The blue region is the region of unconditional stability for linear equations: \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\) (COOK (11.13-7), PDF p. 433, not proved here). We shall prove less, but enough for our use, namely for the line of the family \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\), which lies inside the region at \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\), because \(\beta - \gamma/2 = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4 - \gamma/2 = (\gamma - \tfrac12)^2/4 \ge 0\), so \(2\beta \ge \gamma\). On it also lie \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) with \(\beta = 0{,}3025\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) with \(\beta = 0{,}36\), which we shall compare with the trapezoidal rule. The reason for this line is in the step that we compute now.

17.8.2 The step for one mode (Korak za en način)

As with the trapezoidal rule we test the scheme on one mode, since at \(\mat C = \mat 0\) and \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) it splits by modes. Mode \(r\) has the eigenpair \((\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})\) of theorem 10.21, the coordinate \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\). The quantity \(p\) has the same unit as \(\eta\), so we can build one column \((\eta, p)\) from the two. The scheme takes a step with this column as with a matrix \(\mat A\) that has two rows and two columns. The reader knows the matrix, its trace (sled, the sum of the diagonal elements) and its determinant. An eigenvalue of the matrix \(\mat A\) is a number \(\lambda\) for which the equation \(\mat A\vek x = \lambda\vek x\) has a nonzero solution. For two rows these two numbers are the roots of the equation \(\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}\mat A)\,\lambda + \det\mat A = 0\). Why: a nonzero solution of \((\mat A - \lambda\mat I)\vek x = \vek 0\) exists only if the determinant of that matrix is zero, \((A_{11} - \lambda)(A_{22} - \lambda) - A_{12}A_{21} = 0\), and expanding gives exactly the equation above. By Vieta's formulas the product of the eigenvalues is therefore \(\det\mat A\) and their sum is \(\operatorname{tr}\mat A\). The spectral radius (spektralni polmer) \(\rho(\mat A)\) is the largest absolute value among the eigenvalues. It is called a radius because all eigenvalues lie in the complex plane in the disc of this radius around the origin. Writing it with the matrix, \(\rho(\mat A)\), tells it apart from the density \(\rho\) of other chapters. In figure 17.62 the state of a mode is a point in the \((\eta, p)\) plane and the step is an arrow to the next point.

Figure 17.62 shows what one step does to a mode. On the left we draw the \((\eta, p)\) plane and in it the state \((\eta_{\mathrm{k}}, p_{\mathrm{k}})\) as a point with a vector from the origin. The step is an arrow to the next point: the matrix \(\mat A\) rotates the state and changes its length. If we repeat the step, the points form a spiral that narrows when the length after a step is below one, and a spiral that widens when it is above. On the right we draw the unit circle in the plane of eigenvalues. The eigenvalues \(\rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) are conjugate points, the length \(\rho\) is their distance from the origin and the angle \(\varphi\) is the rotation per step. At \(\rho < 1\) they lie inside the circle and the spiral narrows, at \(\rho > 1\) they lie outside the circle and it widens.

Lemma 17.38 One step of the Newmark scheme in one mode (Korak Newmarkove sheme v enem načinu)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be positive definite, \(\mat C = \mat 0\), \(\vek Q = \vek 0\), \(\beta \ge 0\), \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\) and \(D = 1 + \beta\Omega^2\). For the Newmark scheme (definition 17.36) for the step of the state we have

\[\begin{pmatrix}\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}+1} \\ p_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}+1}\end{pmatrix} = \mat A\begin{pmatrix}\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} \\ p_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}\end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat A = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1 - (\frac12 - \beta)\Omega^2}{D} & \dfrac{\Omega}{D} \\[2mm] -\Omega(1 - \gamma) - \gamma\Omega A_{11} & 1 - \dfrac{\gamma\Omega^2}{D}\end{pmatrix} , \tag{17.35}\]

where \(A_{11}\) is the element at the top left, and

\[\operatorname{tr}\mat A = 2 - \frac{(\gamma + \frac12)\,\Omega^2}{D} , \qquad \det\mat A = 1 - \frac{(\gamma - \frac12)\,\Omega^2}{D} . \tag{17.36}\]
Proof

We show that equations (17.33) and (17.34) are written by modes with the matrix \(\mat A\), and then we compute the trace and the determinant.

  1. We multiply equations (17.33) and (17.34) by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\). As in step 1 of the proof of theorem 10.96, \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}\). The first equation gives \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \eta_{\mathrm{k}} + \Omega\,p_{\mathrm{k}} - \Omega^2\big((\tfrac12 - \beta)\eta_{\mathrm{k}} + \beta\,\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\big)\), the second after division by \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) gives \(p_{\mathrm{k}+1} = p_{\mathrm{k}} - \Omega\big((1 - \gamma)\eta_{\mathrm{k}} + \gamma\,\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\big)\) (we drop the index \(r\)).
  2. We solve the first equation for \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\): \(D\,\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \big(1 - (\tfrac12 - \beta)\Omega^2\big)\eta_{\mathrm{k}} + \Omega\,p_{\mathrm{k}}\). This is the first row of matrix (17.35).
  3. We insert \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) into the second equation. The coefficient of \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(-\Omega(1 - \gamma) - \gamma\Omega A_{11}\), and that of \(p_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(1 - \gamma\Omega\cdot\Omega/D\). This is the second row.
  4. Trace: \(A_{11} + A_{22} = \dfrac{1 - (\frac12 - \beta)\Omega^2 + D - \gamma\Omega^2}{D} = \dfrac{2 + (2\beta - \frac12 - \gamma)\Omega^2}{D}\). Since \(2D = 2 + 2\beta\Omega^2\), this is \(2 - (\gamma + \frac12)\Omega^2/D\).
  5. Determinant: \(A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21}\). The product \(A_{12}A_{21} = -\dfrac{\Omega^2(1 - \gamma)}{D} - \dfrac{\gamma\Omega^2}{D}A_{11}\), and the product \(A_{11}A_{22} = A_{11} - \dfrac{\gamma\Omega^2}{D}A_{11}\). The terms with \(\gamma\Omega^2A_{11}/D\) cancel in the subtraction and what remains is \(\det\mat A = A_{11} + \dfrac{\Omega^2(1 - \gamma)}{D} = \dfrac{1 + (\frac12 + \beta - \gamma)\Omega^2}{D}\). Since \(D + (\frac12 - \gamma)\Omega^2 = 1 + (\beta + \frac12 - \gamma)\Omega^2\), this is \(1 - (\gamma - \frac12)\Omega^2/D\).

Source: COOK §11.14 (PDF pp. 437 to 439) analyses the same with one mode and the roots of the characteristic equation. Equations (17.35) and (17.36) are ours (SymPy, outlines/ch-modeliranje/num-08.py, part S1, which checks both differences against zero).

The trace and the determinant fix the eigenvalues. For the trapezoidal rule (\(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = \tfrac14\)) the determinant is \(1\) and the eigenvalues are \(\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\,2\arctan(\Omega/2)}\) by theorem 10.96. What does a determinant that is not \(1\) do? The eigenvalues are conjugate numbers \(\lambda = \rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) and their product is \(\rho^2 = \det\mat A\). As point 2 of the theorem below shows, every step therefore multiplies the size of the oscillation by \(\rho\) and shifts its phase by \(\varphi\). At \(\det\mat A < 1\) the oscillation decays, at \(\det\mat A > 1\) it grows. The eigenvalues, however, are not necessarily conjugate: for a positive discriminant \((\operatorname{tr}\mat A)^2 - 4\det\mat A\) they are real, and then one of them can exceed \(1\) in absolute value even when \(\det\mat A < 1\). At \(\beta = (\gamma + \frac12)^2/4\) this cannot happen, as the theorem shows. In figure 17.62 the eigenvalues \(\rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) are conjugate points, and the spiral narrows at \(\rho < 1\).

Theorem 17.39 Stability of the Newmark scheme at \(\beta = (\gamma + \frac12)^2/4\) (Stabilnost Newmarkove sheme)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be positive definite, \(\mat C = \mat 0\), \(\vek Q = \vek 0\), \(\gamma\) a real number and \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\). For every mode \(r\) and every \(\Delta t > 0\) with \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\):

  1. The discriminant of the matrix \(\mat A\) of lemma 17.38 is \((\operatorname{tr}\mat A)^2 - 4\det\mat A = -4\Omega^2/D^2 < 0\), so the eigenvalues are conjugate numbers \(\rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) with \(\varphi \in (0, \pi)\) and
    \[\rho(\mat A)^2 = \det\mat A = 1 - \frac{(\gamma - \frac12)\,\Omega^2}{1 + \beta\,\Omega^2} . \tag{17.37}\]
  2. For every start there are numbers \(R\) and \(\delta\) such that \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = R\,\rho^k\cos(k\varphi - \delta)\) for every \(k \ge 0\). At \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\) we therefore have \(|\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}| \le R\) for every \(k\), and the scheme is unconditionally stable in the sense of definition 10.94. This is the spiral with the radius \(\rho\) per step.
  3. At \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho > 1\) at every \(\Omega > 0\), and the scheme is not stable at any step. Then the eigenvalues lie outside the circle and the spiral widens.
  4. The point \((\gamma, \beta)\) lies in the region \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\) of figure 17.61 exactly when \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\).
Proof

We show that the conjugate eigenvalues have the product \(\rho^2\) and that the recursion of lemma 10.98 then describes every mode.

  1. With \(g = \gamma + \tfrac12\) we have \(\beta = g^2/4\), so \(4\beta\Omega^2 = g^2\Omega^2 = 4(D - 1)\). By equation (17.36), \(\operatorname{tr}\mat A = 2 - g\Omega^2/D\) and \(\det\mat A = 1 - (g - 1)\Omega^2/D\). The discriminant is \(\big(2 - \tfrac{g\Omega^2}{D}\big)^2 - 4\big(1 - \tfrac{(g - 1)\Omega^2}{D}\big) = -\tfrac{4\Omega^2}{D} + \tfrac{g^2\Omega^4}{D^2} = \tfrac{\Omega^2}{D^2}\big(g^2\Omega^2 - 4D\big)\). Since \(g^2\Omega^2 = 4D - 4\), this is \(-4\Omega^2/D^2 < 0\). Hence \((\operatorname{tr}\mat A)^2 < 4\det\mat A\), so \(\det\mat A > 0\) and the eigenvalues are conjugate numbers with nonzero imaginary part. Their product is \(|\lambda|^2 = \rho^2 = \det\mat A\), which gives equation (17.37). The angle \(\varphi \in (0, \pi)\) is the angle of the eigenvalue with positive imaginary part, \(\cos\varphi = \operatorname{tr}\mat A/(2\rho)\). So the eigenvalues are conjugate points off the real axis.
  2. For a matrix with two rows, \(\mat A^2 - (\operatorname{tr}\mat A)\,\mat A + (\det\mat A)\,\mat I = \mat 0\) (direct multiplication of the elements). We apply this identity to the column \((\eta_{\mathrm{k}-1}, p_{\mathrm{k}-1})^\T\): for \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}}\) and also for \(p_{\mathrm{k}}\) we get \(u_{\mathrm{k}+1} - (\operatorname{tr}\mat A)\,u_{\mathrm{k}} + \rho^2\,u_{\mathrm{k}-1} = 0\) at \(k \ge 1\). With \(u_{\mathrm{k}} = \rho^k w_{\mathrm{k}}\) and division by \(\rho^{k+1}\) we get \(w_{\mathrm{k}+1} - 2b\,w_{\mathrm{k}} + w_{\mathrm{k}-1} = 0\) with \(b = \operatorname{tr}\mat A/(2\rho)\) and \(|b| < 1\), because \((\operatorname{tr}\mat A)^2 < 4\rho^2\). By point 1 of lemma 10.98, \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = w_0\cos k\psi + c\sin k\psi\) with \(\cos\psi = b\) and \(\psi \in (0, \pi)\), so \(\psi = \varphi\). With \(w_0\cos k\varphi + c\sin k\varphi = R\cos(k\varphi - \delta)\) and \(R = \sqrt{w_0^2 + c^2}\) we get \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}} = R\rho^k\cos(k\varphi - \delta)\). The sequence \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the spiral seen along one coordinate.
  3. At \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\) equation (17.37) gives \(\rho \le 1\), so \(|\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}| \le R_{\mathrm{r}}\) for every \(r\) and every \(k\). By corollary 10.22, \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \eta_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{k}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), and by \(\mat M\)-orthonormality \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}}\eta_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{k}}^2 \le \sum_{\mathrm{s}} R_{\mathrm{s}}^2\). This is the bound \(B\) of definition 10.94 and it does not depend on \(k\). At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho = 1\), the amplitude is constant (as after theorem 10.95). At \(\rho \le 1\) the eigenvalues lie in the disc or on the circle, so the spiral stays bounded.
  4. Point 3. At \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) we have \(\det\mat A > 1\), so \(\rho > 1\). Start with \(\vek q_0 = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\vek v_0 = \vek 0\), so \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},0} = 1\), \(p_{\mathrm{r},0} = 0\), and \(R \ge 1\). If \(\cos(k\varphi - \delta) \to 0\), then \(|\sin(k\varphi - \delta)| \to 1\) and \(\cos((k+1)\varphi - \delta) = \cos(k\varphi - \delta)\cos\varphi - \sin(k\varphi - \delta)\sin\varphi\) would have an absolute value tending to \(\sin\varphi \ne 0\), which is a contradiction. Hence \(|\cos(k\varphi - \delta)| \ge \varepsilon > 0\) for infinitely many \(k\), and \(|\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}| \ge R\rho^k\varepsilon\) is not bounded. Since \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} \ge \eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}^2\), the scheme is not stable by definition 10.94. Then the eigenvalues lie outside the circle and the spiral runs away.
  5. Point 4. From \(\beta - \gamma/2 = (\gamma - \tfrac12)^2/4 \ge 0\) we have \(2\beta \ge \gamma\) at every \(\gamma\), so the condition \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\) is the same as \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\). The line of the family lies in the region of figure 17.61.

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 433), (11.13-7): unconditional stability at \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\), stated there without proof, with a reference to the literature. The choice \(\beta = \tfrac14(\gamma + \tfrac12)^2\) is COOK (11.13-10), PDF p. 434: the best damping of high frequencies while unconditional stability is kept. The proof for this line, the splitting by modes and the recursion are ours. The general region of (11.13-7) is not proved here.

Point 2 of the theorem is what we obtained for the trapezoidal rule from one complex number: the size of the oscillation in mode \(r\) is multiplied by \(\rho\) after every step and the phase is turned by \(\varphi\). At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho = 1\), at \(\gamma > \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho < 1\), at \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho > 1\). This is not conditional stability as with central differences. The scheme at \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) inflates every oscillation at every step. We see it in figure 17.62: narrowing spirals at \(\rho < 1\), widening ones at \(\rho > 1\), and the circle at \(\rho = 1\).

Definition 17.40 Numerical damping (Numerično dušenje)

Let the Newmark scheme at \(\mat C = \mat 0\) satisfy theorem 17.39 and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{r}} = \rho(\mat A)\) be the spectral radius of the step in mode \(r\) at \(\Omega_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\). The scheme has numerical damping (numerično dušenje, in COOK algorithmic damping) in mode \(r\) if \(\rho_{\mathrm{r}} < 1\). The number In figure 17.63 this is a curve below the value \(1\).

\[\zeta_{\mathrm{num},\mathrm{r}} = -\frac{\ln\rho_{\mathrm{r}}}{\Omega_{\mathrm{r}}} \tag{17.38}\]

is the numerical damping ratio of mode \(r\).

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 433 to 434): "algorithmic damping", at \(\gamma > \tfrac12\). The ratio \(\zeta_{\mathrm{num}}\) is ours: the reason is that viscous damping with ratio \(\zeta\) reduces the size of a mode after time \(\Delta t\) by \(\mathrm{e}^{-\zeta\omega\Delta t}\) (section 10.10.2), and the scheme after one step by \(\rho_{\mathrm{r}}\), which is the same at \(\zeta = \zeta_{\mathrm{num},\mathrm{r}}\).

The name says that the damping does not come from the structure but from the computing procedure: it is not in the matrix \(\mat C\) and we cannot assign it to any mechanism. The damping that comes from the structure is treated in chapter 20. In figure 17.63 the curve falls below \(1\) although \(\mat C = \mat 0\).

Corollary 17.41 Numerical damping of high and low modes (Numerično dušenje visokih in nizkih načinov)

Let \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\) and \(\tfrac12 < \gamma \le \tfrac32\). The spectral radius \(\rho(\mat A)\) of equation (17.37) is a decreasing function of the number \(\Omega\) with the limits Figure 17.63 shows them as the curves at \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}7\).

\[\rho(\mat A) \to 1 \ \ (\Omega \to 0) , \qquad \rho(\mat A) \to \frac{\tfrac32 - \gamma}{\gamma + \tfrac12} \ \ (\Omega \to \infty) . \tag{17.39}\]

At small \(\Omega\) we have \(\rho(\mat A)^2 = 1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)\,\Omega^2 + O(\Omega^4)\).

Proof

We show that the fraction \(h(\Omega) = \Omega^2/(1 + \beta\Omega^2)\) in equation (17.37) is increasing and has the limit \(1/\beta\).

  1. We have \(h = \tfrac1\beta\big(1 - \tfrac{1}{1 + \beta\Omega^2}\big)\). The fraction \(1/(1 + \beta\Omega^2)\) decreases with \(\Omega\) towards \(0\), so \(h\) increases from \(0\) towards \(1/\beta\).
  2. Hence \(\rho^2 = 1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)\,h\) decreases from \(1\) towards \(1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)/\beta = 1 - \dfrac{4(\gamma - \frac12)}{(\gamma + \frac12)^2}\). Since \((\gamma + \tfrac12)^2 - 4\gamma + 2 = \gamma^2 - 3\gamma + \tfrac94 = (\gamma - \tfrac32)^2\), this limit is \(\dfrac{(\gamma - \frac32)^2}{(\gamma + \frac12)^2}\), so the limit of \(\rho\) is \((\tfrac32 - \gamma)/(\gamma + \tfrac12)\) at \(\gamma \le \tfrac32\). In figure 17.63 this is the fall of the curve to the dashed limit.
  3. Expansion: \(h = \Omega^2 - \beta\Omega^4 + \dots\) (the series for \(1/(1 + s)\) with remainder \(s^2/(1+s)\), \(s = \beta\Omega^2\)), from which \(\rho^2 = 1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)\Omega^2 + O(\Omega^4)\).

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 433 to 434): "when \(\gamma > \tfrac12\), Newmark methods display algorithmic damping, at the cost of reducing guaranteed accuracy from second-order to first-order", and the choice (11.13-10). The limit at \(\Omega \to \infty\) and the expansion are not in the source. The proof is ours (SymPy, num-08.py, parts S1 and S2).

The expansion also tells why COOK says that damping costs one order of accuracy. The size is multiplied in every step by \(\rho \approx 1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)\Omega^2/2\) (from \(\sqrt{1 - x} \approx 1 - x/2\) at small \(x\)), and there are about \(2\pi/\Omega\) steps per oscillation, so the size after one oscillation falls by about \(\pi(\gamma - \tfrac12)\,\Omega\). This loss is proportional to \(\Omega\), that is to the step \(\Delta t\) in the first power, and is therefore of first order. At the trapezoidal rule (\(\gamma = \tfrac12\)) the loss is zero, and the second order stays in the phase (theorem 10.96). Such is the dot on the curve at \(2\pi/20\) in figure 17.63: the loss per oscillation is the gap from \(1\).

Example 17.42 How much the amplitude is reduced (Koliko se zmanjša obseg)

A mode with \(\Omega = 2\pi/20 = 0{,}31416\), that is \(20\) steps per oscillation, has at \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) (\(\beta = 0{,}3025\)) the spectral radius \(0{,}99520\) and after \(20\) steps the size \(0{,}99520^{20} = 0{,}9082\) of the initial one. The numerical damping ratio by equation (17.38) is \(0{,}01533\). At \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) (\(\beta = 0{,}36\)) we have \(\rho = 0{,}99042\), the size after \(20\) steps \(0{,}8249\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{num}} = 0{,}03063\). The same mode with the same step loses nothing at the trapezoidal rule. A mode with \(\Omega = 10\), that is \(0{,}63\) steps per oscillation, has at \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) after one step \(0{,}82462\) and \(0{,}67783\) of the previous size, and at \(\Omega = 1000\) it has \(0{,}81818\) and \(0{,}66667\), which are the limits \((\tfrac32 - \gamma)/(\gamma + \tfrac12)\) of equation (17.39). The values are in the table (NumPy, num-08.py, part S2). The same numbers are the dots on the vertical line \(2\pi/20\) in figure 17.63.

\(\omega\Delta t\) \(0{,}1\) \(2\pi/20\) \(1\) \(10\) \(1000\)
\(\gamma = 0{,}5\), \(\beta = 0{,}25\) \(1{,}00000\) \(1{,}00000\) \(1{,}00000\) \(1{,}00000\) \(1{,}00000\)
\(\gamma = 0{,}6\), \(\beta = 0{,}3025\) \(0{,}99950\) \(0{,}99520\) \(0{,}96085\) \(0{,}82462\) \(0{,}81818\)
\(\gamma = 0{,}7\), \(\beta = 0{,}36\) \(0{,}99900\) \(0{,}99042\) \(0{,}92355\) \(0{,}67783\) \(0{,}66667\)

Figure 17.63 shows the same numbers. We draw the horizontal axis \(\omega\Delta t\) on a logarithmic scale and the vertical axis \(\rho(\mat A)\). The scale is logarithmic because we care about modes from an oscillation with several hundred steps to an oscillation with a part of a step, which is a range of several orders of magnitude. The trapezoidal rule gives a horizontal line at \(1\): it damps no mode. The curve \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) lies on \(1\) at small \(\omega\Delta t\), falls around \(\omega\Delta t \approx 2\) and settles at the dashed limit \(0{,}818\). The curve \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) falls lower and settles at \(0{,}667\). The vertical line at \(2\pi/20\) is the case of the example above, where the curves cut the line in the dots at \(0{,}995\) and \(0{,}990\).

Why damp at all? The highest modes of a mesh have frequencies that are poorly determined: the order of the error from corollary 10.54 holds at fixed \(r\) and falling \(h\), not for the highest modes of the mesh. These modes are often not part of what we care about, and boundary conditions or a sudden load can excite them. COOK gives this as the reason for numerical damping: to damp high modes that are "of little interest or constitute only undesirable nonphysical oscillations associated with discretization" (COOK PDF p. 434). Adding viscous damping raises \(\zeta\), but according to Hughes, whom COOK cites, with the trapezoidal rule it may damp mostly the middle modes, while the highest and the lowest stay almost untouched (COOK PDF p. 434). Numerical damping with the curves of figure 17.63 is therefore the better choice: it damps the more the higher the frequency.

The figure also shows the price. At \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) a mode with \(20\) steps per oscillation is reduced to \(82{,}5\) % in one oscillation, which is about a damping ratio of \(3\) %, and this is not in the model. Whoever compares the measured damping of a structure with the response of a computation with \(\gamma > \tfrac12\) compares the measured value with only a part of the computed damping. For this reason \(\gamma\) is kept near \(\tfrac12\), and at \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) the damping is \(1{,}5\) %. COOK also names the \(\alpha\)-method (Hilber, Hughes and Taylor), which keeps the damping in high modes and reduces it in low ones, without losing the second order (COOK PDF p. 433 to 434). That scheme is only named here. The opposite direction is more dangerous still: at \(\gamma = 0{,}4\) (\(\beta = 0{,}2025\)) we have \(\rho > 1\) by theorem 17.39, point 3, and a mode with \(\Omega = 2\pi/20\) grows after \(20\) steps to \(1{,}1011\) of its size, and at \(\Omega = 10\) by a factor \(1{,}2127\) per step (num-08.py, part S5). A scheme with \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) is therefore not inaccurate but wrong. At \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) it is the lower curve, at \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) the higher one.

17.8.3 The nonlinear step (Nelinearni korak)

So far the force was linear, \(\mat K\vek q\). A nonlinear system has an internal force \(\vek f(\vek q)\) that is no longer linear, and the equation of motion \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \vek f(\vek q) = \vek Q(t)\) (a conservative system without damping). For \(\vek f = \mat K\vek q\) we get the previous equation. The Newmark equations (17.33) and (17.34) stay, because they speak only of displacement, velocity and acceleration. At \(\beta > 0\) we express from the first the acceleration at the end of the step through the unknown \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\),

\[\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \frac{\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} - \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} - \Delta t^2(\frac12 - \beta)\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}}{\beta\,\Delta t^2} , \tag{17.40}\]

and insert it in the equation of motion at the end of the step. An equation for one unknown remains, \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\),

\[\vek G(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = \mat M\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}) + \vek f(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}) - \vek Q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek 0 . \tag{17.41}\]

For a linear \(\vek f = \mat K\vek q\) this is a linear equation with the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}} = \mat K + \mat M/(\beta\Delta t^2)\), and at \(\beta = \tfrac14\) and \(\mat C = \mat 0\) it is exactly equation (10.121). In the nonlinear case we solve it with Newton's method from section 17.7 (definition 17.32): from an approximation \(\vek q^{(i)}\) we get the next one with

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}^{(i)}\,\Delta\vek q = -\vek G\big(\vek q^{(i)}\big) , \qquad \mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}^{(i)} = \mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\big(\vek q^{(i)}\big) + \frac{\mat M}{\beta\,\Delta t^2} , \tag{17.42}\]

where \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is the tangent stiffness (definition 17.31) and \(\Delta\vek q\) the correction of the approximation. We start with the approximation from the start of the step, \(\vek q^{(0)} = \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t^2(\tfrac12 - \beta)\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\), that is with the displacement that equation (17.33) would give at \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek 0\). A warning about the cost: the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}^{(i)}\) changes with \(\vek q^{(i)}\), so the factorization of the matrix (lemma 7.47), which we did once for all steps in the linear system (chapter 10), is repeated here at every iteration of every step. This is the cost of nonlinearity (section 17.6 treats large systems). We stop the iterations when the correction is smaller than \(\delta\) (section 17.7), and this stopping is the numerical error of definition 17.2. Each correction is a step along the tangent to the axis, as figure 17.64 shows.

Figure 17.64 shows the Newton method for one unknown. We draw the \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) axis and the \(G\) axis and the curve \(G\), whose zero is the wanted solution of the step. We start at the guess \(q^{(0)}\). The tangent at that point has the slope \(K_{\mathrm{ef}}^{(0)}\) and meets the axis at the next guess \(q^{(1)}\). From it we draw a new tangent and arrive at \(q^{(2)}\), which is already hardly distinguishable from the zero.

Does equation (17.41) have a solution at all, and one only? We show this on the pendulum, where the unknown is one angle.

Lemma 17.43 The step equation for the pendulum (Enačba koraka za nihalo)

Let the pendulum (\(\ddot\theta = -\sin\theta\), time in units of \(\sqrt{l/g}\)) make a step \(\Delta t\) with the trapezoidal rule (\(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = \tfrac14\)) from the state \((\theta_{\mathrm{k}}, v_{\mathrm{k}}, a_{\mathrm{k}})\). The equation for \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) is \(g(\theta) = \theta - c + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\sin\theta = 0\) with \(c = \theta_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}a_{\mathrm{k}}\). At \(\Delta t < 2\) it has exactly one solution. At \(\Delta t > 2\) there may be more solutions. Figure 17.65 shows one zero at a small step and three at a large one.

Proof

We show that at \(\Delta t < 2\) the function \(g\) is strictly increasing and unbounded in both directions, and that this does not hold for a larger step.

  1. From equation (17.40) at \(\beta = \tfrac14\) and \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = -\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) it follows that \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \theta_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\big(a_{\mathrm{k}} - \sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\big)\), which is \(g(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = 0\). This is the equation whose zero is the solution of the step.
  2. The derivative is \(g'(\theta) = 1 + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\cos\theta \ge 1 - \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\). At \(\Delta t < 2\) this is a positive number, so \(g\) is strictly increasing (mean value theorem). Such is the almost straight curve in figure 17.65.
  3. Since \(|\sin\theta| \le 1\), we have \(g(\theta) \ge \theta - c - \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\) and \(g(\theta) \le \theta - c + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\). So \(g < 0\) at small enough and \(g > 0\) at large enough \(\theta\). A continuous, strictly increasing function that changes sign has by the intermediate value theorem exactly one zero. So the curve crosses the axis \(g = 0\) at one point.
  4. At \(\Delta t > 2\) we have \(g'(\theta) < 0\) where \(\cos\theta < -4/\Delta t^2\), so \(g\) is not monotonic and may have several zeros. An example is in the example below. Such is the orange curve with three zeros.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

An example with numbers. The pendulum from the position \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}} = \pi/2\) with \(v_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) and \(a_{\mathrm{k}} = -1\) has \(c = \pi/2 - \Delta t^2/4\). Figure 17.65 shows the function \(g\). We draw the axis \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) and the axis \(g\), where a zero means a solution. At \(\Delta t = 2\pi/20 = 0{,}31416\) we have \(g' \ge 0{,}9753\), the blue curve is almost a straight line and has one zero at \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1} = 1{,}5215\). At \(\Delta t = 4\) it is no longer monotonic: the orange curve has three zeros at \(-5{,}4335\), \(-3{,}3821\) and \(-0{,}5026\) (num-08.py, part S5). The step \(\Delta t = 4\) is useless for computing the oscillation, since the period at small deflections is \(2\pi \approx 6{,}28\), fewer than two steps per oscillation, but it shows that unconditional stability in the linear case is not a property of the scheme on the nonlinear equation: there the step is not even uniquely determined. What matters most to us is that at this step Newton's method finds one of the three zeros, depending on the initial approximation, and not necessarily the one we want. Similarly, in section 17.7 at a load above the limit force it found an equilibrium that is not stable.

17.8.4 The pendulum (Nihalo)

The model is a point mass on a rigid weightless rod of length \(l\) in the gravity field \(g\) with the angle \(\theta\) from the vertical, without friction in the axis and without air drag. The equation of motion is \(\ddot\theta = -(g/l)\sin\theta\) (theorem 8.139). For time we take the unit \(\sqrt{l/g}\), and the equation is \(\theta'' + \sin\theta = 0\) (the prime is the derivative with respect to dimensionless time). This is equation (17.41) with \(M = 1\), \(f(\theta) = \sin\theta\), \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = \cos\theta\) and \(Q = 0\). We start from \(\theta_0 = \pi/2\), \(v_0 = 0\) and use the trapezoidal rule with Newton at every step. By theorem 8.139 the exact period at amplitude \(90°\) is \(T = 4\int_0^{\pi/2}\big(1 - \tfrac12\sin^2u\big)^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}u = 7{,}41630\) (NumPy, arithmetic-geometric mean), at small amplitude \(2\pi = 6{,}28319\). At \(l = 1\) m and \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s\(^2\) the unit of time is \(0{,}3193\) s, and \(T = 2{,}368\) s. The rod with the mass at its end is in figure 17.66.

Figure 17.66 shows the model. We draw the pivot and from it the rigid rod of length \(l\). At its end is the point mass \(m\). The vertical through the pivot is the measure of the deflection and the angle \(\theta\) is the rotation of the rod from it. On the mass acts the weight \(mg\) downwards.

Figure 17.67 shows three oscillations. We draw the time axis and the axis of deflection \(\theta\) with the limits \(\pm\pi/2\). The grey curve is the exact solution, computed with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method with the step \(3T/20000 \approx 0{,}0011\), about \(565\) times smaller than the step of the scheme (fig-08.py), so the difference is zero to the accuracy of drawing. The blue dots are the values of the trapezoidal rule with step \(2\pi/10\), which is deliberately coarse here so that the error is visible. The dots lag behind the curve: the scheme slows the pendulum down. The cause is already known from theorem 10.96: the trapezoidal rule turns the phase by \(2\arctan(\Omega/2)\) instead of \(\Omega\), and the period in the scheme is therefore longer. The pendulum at amplitude \(90°\) has a frequency lower than \(1\), namely \(2\pi/T = 0{,}84721\). With it \(x = 0{,}84721\cdot 2\pi/20/2 = 0{,}13308\) and \(x/\arctan x - 1 = 0{,}588\) %, which is close to the measured \(0{,}57\) % at step \(2\pi/20\). The linear formula of chapter 10 therefore predicts the error well also for the nonlinear pendulum (table below).

The results with three smaller steps are in the table. At every step Newton needed at most \(3\) iterations (\(4\) at \(\Delta t = 2\pi/10\)), stopping at a correction below \(10^{-12}\). The last column is the largest deviation of the energy \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12v_{\mathrm{k}}^2 + 1 - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\) from the initial value \(\mathcal{E}_0 = 1\) in three oscillations. Figure 17.69 shows the same deviations as three curves.

\(\Delta t\) period error iterations per step \(\max\lvert\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} - 1\rvert\)
\(2\pi/10\) \(7{,}58203\) \(2{,}23\) % \(4\) \(3{,}05\cdot 10^{-2}\)
\(2\pi/20\) \(7{,}45854\) \(0{,}57\) % \(3\) \(8{,}06\cdot 10^{-3}\)
\(2\pi/40\) \(7{,}42673\) \(0{,}14\) % \(3\) \(2{,}05\cdot 10^{-3}\)
\(2\pi/80\) \(7{,}41890\) \(0{,}04\) % \(3\) \(5{,}13\cdot 10^{-4}\)

The error of the period falls about four times when the step is halved, which is second order. The same holds for the energy. In a linear system the trapezoidal rule conserves the energy exactly (theorem 10.95). For the pendulum it does not, and not because of rounding: even the smallest difference in the table, \(5{,}13\cdot 10^{-4}\), is more than ten orders of magnitude above rounding, which is about \(10^{-16}\). Why is shown by a computation that repeats the proof of theorem 10.95 and stops where the force is no longer linear. We do it for a general force \(f\) and one degree of freedom. For the energy this is the difference between the curves in figure 17.69.

Figure 17.68 shows the force \(f\) between \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). We draw the curve of the force and under it the area, which is \(\int f\,\mathrm{d}s\), the change of the potential energy. The trapezoidal formula replaces it by the trapezoid under the chord between \(f(q_{\mathrm{k}})\) and \(f(q_{\mathrm{k}+1})\), with the width \(h_{\mathrm{k}}\). Since \(f\) is curved, the chord does not follow the curve and a thin sliver remains between them: this is the error of the trapezoidal formula.

Theorem 17.44 Energy of the trapezoidal rule for a nonlinear force (Energija trapeznega pravila pri nelinearni sili)

Let \(f\) be a twice continuously differentiable function, \(V\) its antiderivative (\(V' = f\)), \(\ddot q + f(q) = 0\) the equation of motion of unit mass, and let the trapezoidal rule (definition 10.92) with step \(\Delta t\) give the sequence \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{k}} = -f(q_{\mathrm{k}})\). With \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12v_{\mathrm{k}}^2 + V(q_{\mathrm{k}})\) and \(h_{\mathrm{k}} = q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - q_{\mathrm{k}}\) we have

\[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \int_{\mathrm{q}_\mathrm{k}}^{q_{\mathrm{k}+1}}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s - \frac{h_{\mathrm{k}}}{2}\big(f(q_{\mathrm{k}}) + f(q_{\mathrm{k}+1})\big) , \tag{17.43}\]

and this difference is in absolute value at most \(\dfrac{\lvert h_{\mathrm{k}}\rvert^3}{12}\max\lvert f''\rvert\), where the maximum is over the interval between \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). For a linear \(f\) the difference is zero. The difference is the error of the trapezoidal formula for the area under the force.

Proof

We show that the increment of energy is the error of the trapezoidal formula for the integral of the force.

  1. Kinetic part: \(\tfrac12(v_{\mathrm{k}+1}^2 - v_{\mathrm{k}}^2) = \tfrac12(v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + v_{\mathrm{k}})(v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - v_{\mathrm{k}})\). By equation (10.119) we have \(v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - v_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(a_{\mathrm{k}} + a_{\mathrm{k}+1})\), and by equation (10.118) \(\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(v_{\mathrm{k}} + v_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = h_{\mathrm{k}}\). So the kinetic part is \(\tfrac12h_{\mathrm{k}}(a_{\mathrm{k}} + a_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = -\tfrac{h_{\mathrm{k}}}{2}\big(f(q_{\mathrm{k}}) + f(q_{\mathrm{k}+1})\big)\). This is minus the area of the trapezoid.
  2. Potential part: \(V(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}) - V(q_{\mathrm{k}}) = \int_{\mathrm{q}_\mathrm{k}}^{q_{\mathrm{k}+1}}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) by the fundamental theorem of calculus. The sum of steps 1 and 2 is equation (17.43). This is the area under the force.
  3. Let \(a < b\) be the end points of the interval. Integration by parts twice gives \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b(s - a)(b - s)f''(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = (b - a)\big(f(a) + f(b)\big) - 2\int_{\mathrm{a}}^bf(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\): the first boundary term \((s - a)(b - s)f'\) is zero at the end points, and the second part gives \(-\big[(a + b - 2s)f\big]_{\mathrm{a}}^b - 2\int_{\mathrm{a}}^bf\), which is \((b - a)(f(a) + f(b)) - 2\int_{\mathrm{a}}^bf\).
  4. Hence \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^bf - \tfrac{b - a}{2}(f(a) + f(b)) = -\tfrac12\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b(s - a)(b - s)f''(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). The kernel \((s - a)(b - s)\) is non-negative with integral \((b - a)^3/6\), so the absolute value of the right side is at most \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{(b - a)^3}{6}\max|f''| = \tfrac{(b - a)^3}{12}\max|f''|\). At \(h_{\mathrm{k}} < 0\) we swap the meaning of the end points and the expression for the difference gets the opposite sign, the absolute value stays. For a linear \(f\) we have \(f'' = 0\). We bound the thin sliver between the chord and the curve.

Source: The proof is not from a source. For a linear force it condenses theorem 10.95. The error of the trapezoidal formula is mentioned in COOK (PDF p. 619) only as second order (parameter \(0{,}5\) in the generalized trapezoidal formula (17.3-8)).

For the pendulum \(f = \sin\), \(|f''| \le 1\) and every step changes the energy by at most \(|h_{\mathrm{k}}|^3/12\). This is an upper bound for a single step. The sum of these bounds over three oscillations is \(0{,}708\), \(0{,}192\), \(0{,}049\) and \(0{,}0123\) at the four steps of the table, so it indeed falls four times with every halved step, because \(|h_{\mathrm{k}}| \approx \Delta t\,|v_{\mathrm{k}}|\) and \(|h_{\mathrm{k}}|^3\approx\Delta t^3|v_{\mathrm{k}}|^3\) at \(\sim\!1/\Delta t\) steps. But the bound is too loose, since the actual deviation is \(8{,}06\cdot 10^{-3}\) and not \(0{,}192\). The signs cancel, as figure 17.69 shows. We draw the time axis and the axis of the difference \(\mathcal{E} - \mathcal{E}_0\). At step \(2\pi/20\) (blue) the difference is everywhere negative or near zero, reaches \(-0{,}0081\) at the passage through the lowest position and returns to zero at every turning point: the energy therefore does not drift away but oscillates around the true value at the bottom. The steps \(2\pi/40\) (orange) and \(2\pi/80\) (grey) give the same shape four and sixteen times smaller.

Why does it return to zero? By theorem 17.44 the increment is \(-\tfrac{h_{\mathrm{k}}^3}{12}f''(\xi_{\mathrm{k}})\) with \(f'' = -\sin\) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{k}}\) between \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), so approximately \(+\tfrac{h_{\mathrm{k}}^3}{12}\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\) (this is an estimate, not a theorem: we replace \(\xi_{\mathrm{k}}\) by \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\)). On the way from \(\theta = \pi/2\) towards \(0\) we have \(h_{\mathrm{k}} < 0\) and \(\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\), so the increment is negative. On the way from \(0\) towards \(-\pi/2\) we have \(h_{\mathrm{k}} < 0\) and \(\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}} < 0\), so the increment is positive. We add the first part as a Riemann sum with step \(\Delta t\) and \(h_{\mathrm{k}} \approx \Delta t\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\): \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} h_{\mathrm{k}}^3\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}}/12 \approx \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{12}\int_0^{T/4}v^3\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}t\). For the exact solution, conservation of energy gives \(v^2 = 2\cos\theta\), and with the substitution \(\theta = \theta(t)\), for which \(\theta'(t) = v(t)\), the integral is \(\int_{\pi/2}^{0}2\cos\theta\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -1\) (NumPy, \(40000\) steps: \(-1{,}00000\)). The deviation at the bottom is therefore about \(-\Delta t^2/12 = -0{,}0833\,\Delta t^2\), and the measured values are \(0{,}0817\), \(0{,}0829\) and \(0{,}0832\) times \(\Delta t^2\). The second part of the oscillation brings the same value with the opposite sign, so the energy returns at the turning points. In figure 17.69 this is the bottom of the curve and then the return towards zero.

Such arguments are estimates and not proofs, and the book claims no more than the computation shows: we proved theorem 17.44 (the energy error per step), the quadratic order of the total error we estimated and checked at four steps. For the pendulum \(\max|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} - \mathcal{E}_0|\) is small, but the pendulum is a single mode. In a system with many modes the energy error of every mode is different, and nonlinearity couples them, which this section does not treat. Figure 17.69 shows only the steps of the table.

Example 17.45 An explicit step and a growing stiffness (Eksplicitni korak in rastoča togost)

The unconditional stability of the trapezoidal rule is a property of the linear mode (theorem 17.39). Explicit central differences have the critical step \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = 2/\omega_{\max}\) (theorem 10.99), where \(\omega_{\max}\) is the highest frequency of the system. For a nonlinear force the leading stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) depends on the displacement, so \(\omega_{\max}\) depends on it too. Take the hardening spring \(\ddot q + q + 100\,q^3 = 0\) with \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 1 + 300\,q^2\). At \(q = 0\) we have \(\omega_{\max} = 1\) and \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = 2\). At \(q = 1\) we have \(\omega_{\max} = \sqrt{301} = 17{,}35\) and \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = 0{,}1153\). We start from \(q_0 = 0\) with velocity \(v_0 = 7{,}14\), which has an amplitude around \(1\), and make \(400\) steps of central differences (num-08.py, part S4). At \(\Delta t = 0{,}02\), \(0{,}05\) and \(0{,}08\) the solution stays bounded with the largest deflection \(1{,}0016\), \(1{,}0120\) and \(1{,}0397\). At \(\Delta t = 0{,}1\) and \(0{,}13\) it exceeds \(10^6\) after \(17\) and \(23\) steps. The step \(0{,}1\) is below the critical step at amplitude \(1\), yet the solution escapes: the critical step holds for a given \(\omega_{\max}\), but the deflection in an explicit scheme grows because of inaccuracy to a value where \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) is smaller than the step. This is not a proof for every system, but it is an example of why explicit schemes for nonlinear systems need a reserve below the critical step computed with the largest expected deflection. Figure 17.70 shows the critical step as a function of the deflection: the step \(0{,}1\) is below it at \(q = 1\) but not at a larger deflection.

Figure 17.70 shows why a step that is safe at a small deflection is not at a large one. We draw the axis of the deflection \(q\) and the axis of the step and the curve of the critical step, which falls from \(2\) at \(q = 0\) to \(0{,}1153\) at \(q = 1\). The step \(0{,}1\) is a horizontal line that is below the curve at \(q = 1\). The crossing at \(q = 1{,}15\) is the deflection where the step becomes critical, and there the solution runs away. The step \(0{,}05\) crosses much further out and stays safe.

Figure 17.65 connected the step, the equation and Newton, and figure 17.69 the price we pay for nonlinearity. The section showed three things. In a linear mode the family \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\) keeps stability for every \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\) (theorem 17.39), and the damping of high modes costs one order of accuracy, since the guaranteed accuracy falls from second to first order (corollary 17.41). In the nonlinear step we solve the equation for the unknown displacement with Newton's method, and for the pendulum the step is certainly unique at \(\Delta t < 2\) (lemma 17.43). The trapezoidal rule does not conserve energy for a nonlinear force, and the error per step is given by theorem 17.44. Three proofs (stability of the family, uniqueness of the step and the energy error) we made ourselves, three statements we gave without proof: unconditional stability in the whole region \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\), conditional stability of the linear acceleration scheme and the second order of the \(\alpha\)-method (COOK PDF p. 430 to 434).

17.9 Planning an analysis and the tube case study

The earlier sections of this chapter gave the parts: what a model is (section 17.1), how a body becomes a model (section 17.2), how we check that a result settles down as the mesh is refined (section 17.3), what to do with stresses (section 17.4), when a mesh is bad (section 17.5) and when a system of equations is hard (section 17.6). Whoever carries out an analysis needs an order: what to decide before the first computation, what after it, and when to stop. We call this order the plan of an analysis (načrt analize). In everyday use a plan is a drawing or a sequence of work made before the building starts, and that is what it is here: the decisions we make before the computation so that the computation answers the question we asked.

The plan does not treat only one of the three errors of definition 17.2. It leads us through all three: modelling error (the model against the real body), discretization error (the finite element solution against the exact solution of the model) and numerical error (round-off and stopped iterations). Reducing one does not reduce the others, so the plan separates them and gives each its own step. The steps follow COOK §10.12 to §10.15 (PDF pp. 375-382) and ONATE1 §1.4.4 (PDF pp. 31-33). We test them on the tube of chapter 11, because we know its exact solution and can see what each step tells us and what it does not.

The model is this tube (figure 17.71): a steel wall with inner radius \(a = 40\) mm and outer radius \(b = 60\) mm, modulus \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), oil pressure \(p = 30\) MPa in the bore and a free outer surface (theorem 11.28). The idealizations are the same as there: the material is homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic, and the pressure is uniform over the bore. Linear elasticity holds while the von Mises stress is below the yield stress \(220\) MPa. At \(30\) MPa it will be about \(94\) MPa at the bore, so it holds with a margin, and above the yield pressure the model fails. The ends of the tube are not fixed by the problem. Chapter 11 computed three possibilities, open ends, closed ends and plane strain (definition 11.32), and at \(p = 30\) MPa the von Mises stresses (definition 2.107) at the bore are \(96{,}56\), \(93{,}53\) and \(94{,}02\) MPa. The spread of these three values, \(3{,}2\,\%\), is the price of not knowing the ends. The yield pressure \(p_{\mathrm{Y}}\) is the pressure at which this stress equals the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa of section 2.12.6 of chapter 2, so \(p_{\mathrm{Y}} = 30 \cdot 220/\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\). We carry out the task as if we did not know the exact solution, and compare with it at the end.

On the left of the figure is the cross-section just described, with the dashed cut along a diameter that the hand calculation will need. On the right we draw axes for the hoop stress \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) across the wall from \(a\) to \(b\). By theorem 11.28 it is the curve that falls from \(78\) MPa at the bore to \(48\) MPa at the outer surface. The inner part of the wall thus carries more than the outer part, which is why we look for yielding at the bore.

We build the figure step by step, as one solves the task. First the question: from it follows which quantity we compute and how accurately we need it. For the tube the question is when it starts to yield, and the quantity is the von Mises stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}(a)\) at the bore, because by chapter 11 it is largest there. We choose the accuracy ourselves, \(2\,\%\) for the example, because an error in \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) changes \(p_{\mathrm{Y}}\) by the same fraction. This is our choice for the example and not a datum from a source. For another task the requirement may differ, but it must be written down before the computation, since without it we do not know when the mesh is fine enough.

17.9.1 Question and hand estimate

The second step is the hand calculation, before we open the program. COOK demands it with a good reason: since we find it hard to give up a result that took much work, an approximate result should be ready beforehand, and even a rough calculation detects a displacement in the wrong direction, a strange shape of the field or an error of orders of magnitude (COOK §10.12, PDF p. 375). For the tube the calculation is already in section 11.7.1 of chapter 11. In thought we cut the tube along a diameter and look at the upper half per unit length. The pressure pushes it upwards with the resultant \(2\,p\,a\): the horizontal parts of the pressure from the left and from the right cancel, and the vertical parts add up to the pressure times the width of the bore \(2a\). It is held down by the forces in the two cuts of the wall, each the sum of the hoop stress over the thickness. The half is at rest, so the two forces together equal the resultant (derived at figure 11.69), so

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = p\,a , \tag{17.44}\]

(equation (11.35)). The area under the curve of the hoop stress is therefore \(p\,a = 1{,}2\) MN/m whatever the curve, and the mean hoop stress is \(p\,a/(b - a) = 60\) MPa. With the mean radius in place of \(a\) we get \(75\) MPa (equation (11.36)). The true value at the bore is known from theorem 11.28, \(78\) MPa, and the first two numbers are \(23\,\%\) and \(4\,\%\) below it. The hand calculation here gives the order of magnitude and the sign of the stress, not the stress to \(2\,\%\). Since the two numbers differ from each other by \(25\,\%\), it would catch a factor of \(10\) or a wrong sign, but not finer errors.

The hand calculation and the computer result must refer to the same physical case (COOK §10.15, PDF p. 381). If we compare \(78\) MPa with a mesh that has another pressure or another bore radius, the difference must not be put down to the mesh.

17.9.2 Sequence of models and meshes

The third step is the choice of model. COOK advises a sequence of models from simple to detailed, each correcting the faults of the previous one, because this is faster than one large model that turns out wrong when we look at its result (COOK §10.12, PDF p. 376). For the tube the sequence is: the thin-wall formula (step 2), the Lamé solution, and finally the finite element model. One question remains in the model, the ends of the tube. By theorem 11.28 the constants \(A\) and \(B\), and with them \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\), do not depend on the axial stress \(S\), which enters only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). So the mesh computes the same \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) for all three ends, and the difference of \(3{,}2\,\%\) between \(96{,}56\) and \(93{,}53\) MPa is wholly modelling error. The mesh does not reduce it (definition 17.2), only knowledge of how the tube is really closed decides it.

The computational model is the radial problem of the tube in plane strain with linear elements along the radius, as section 17.4 derives it from the weak form (lemma 17.17). The fourth step is a sequence of meshes with \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\) equal elements. Doubling is not arbitrary: theorem 17.14 needs three nested meshes, each differing from the previous one by the same factor. Example 17.46 collects the results.

Example 17.46 Tube at \(p = 30\) MPa, sequence of meshes (cev, zaporedje mrež)

The values at the inner edge \(r = a\) come from the element at the bore, the stresses from the displacements by Hooke's law, the axial stress from \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta})\) (plane strain), and the exact values are \(u(a) = 16{,}8735\ \mu\)m and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = 94{,}02\) MPa. The error is the difference from the exact value in per cent of that value, and all errors are negative except the error of the hoop stress. The computation is in outlines/ch-modeliranje/num-09.py (NumPy).

\(n\) \(u(a)\) (\(\mu\)m) error of \(u(a)\) \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a)\) (MPa) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}(a)\) (MPa) error of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) \(p_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (MPa)
1 \(16{,}2265\) \(-3{,}834\,\%\) \(88{,}45\) \(76{,}61\) \(-18{,}52\,\%\) \(86{,}15\)
2 \(16{,}6928\) \(-1{,}071\,\%\) \(85{,}35\) \(84{,}41\) \(-10{,}22\,\%\) \(78{,}19\)
4 \(16{,}8268\) \(-0{,}276\,\%\) \(82{,}33\) \(88{,}92\) \(-5{,}42\,\%\) \(74{,}22\)
8 \(16{,}8617\) \(-0{,}070\,\%\) \(80{,}34\) \(91{,}39\) \(-2{,}80\,\%\) \(72{,}22\)
16 \(16{,}8705\) \(-0{,}017\,\%\) \(79{,}22\) \(92{,}68\) \(-1{,}43\,\%\) \(71{,}21\)
32 \(16{,}8727\) \(-0{,}004\,\%\) \(78{,}62\) \(93{,}34\) \(-0{,}72\,\%\) \(70{,}71\)

Figure 17.73 takes two columns of the table. First the axes: horizontally the number of elements \(n\) in doublings, vertically the error in per cent on a logarithmic scale, so a straight line means that the error falls as a power of the element size \(h \sim 1/n\). The blackwhite line is the error of the displacement \(u(a)\): at every doubling it falls to a quarter, which is second order, as section 17.3 predicts for displacements. The blue line is the error of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) at the bore and falls only to a half, so it is first order, because the stress is computed from the derivative of the displacements (section 17.4). The order observed from three consecutive meshes is \(0{,}93\) at \(n = 4, 8, 16\) and \(0{,}96\) at \(n = 8, 16, 32\). The horizontal dashed line at \(2\) is the chosen tolerance: the blue line crosses it between \(n = 8\) (\(2{,}80\,\%\)) and \(n = 16\) (\(1{,}43\,\%\)). The dashed line at \(0{,}53\) is the difference between plane strain and closed ends (\(94{,}02\) against \(93{,}53\) MPa, \(0{,}53\,\%\) of the second value). The blue line is still above it at \(n = 32\), at \(0{,}72\,\%\). The vertical dashed line at \(n = 16\) says one more thing: at this mesh the displacement at the bore is exact to \(0{,}017\,\%\) and the stress to \(1{,}43\,\%\), worse by a factor of \(82\) (from the unrounded errors \(1{,}427\,\%\) and \(0{,}0175\,\%\)). COOK writes this as advice to use a finer mesh for stresses than for displacements (COOK §10.12, PDF p. 376), and the table shows how much finer.

The error has a sign. All the values of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) from the mesh are below the exact one, so the yield pressure \(p_{\mathrm{Y}}\) computed from them is above the true one: at \(n = 16\) it is \(71{,}21\) against \(70{,}20\) MPa. For the question about yielding this is an error on the unsafe side, which is the reason not to stop the mesh at the first number that is close.

17.9.3 Checks and mistakes

The fifth step is the checks of the result. Section 7.10.3 of chapter 7 collected eight of them. For the truss the first is the sum of reactions that balances the load (lemma 7.20). The tube has no supports, so its equivalent check is in half the tube: for the exact field equation (17.44) holds. Does the solution from the mesh satisfy it too? We try it on a mesh of two elements, \(n = 2\), with nodes at \(40\), \(50\) and \(60\) mm.

In the lower part of the figure we draw axes, the radius \(r\) in mm horizontally and the hoop stress vertically. Every element has two Gauss points, and the hoop stress from the mesh there is \(76{,}93\), \(57{,}70\), \(57{,}93\) and \(47{,}44\) MPa. Each point stands for half of its element, \(w_{\mathrm{g}} = 5\) mm, so its contribution to the sum is a column with area stress times \(5\) mm,

\[384{,}6 + 288{,}5 + 289{,}6 + 237{,}2 = 1199{,}9\ \text{N/mm} .\]

With unrounded values the sum is \(1200{,}0\) N/mm, which is \(p\,a = 30\ \text{MPa} \cdot 40\ \text{mm}\). The single columns, however, deviate from the exact curve: at the first Gauss point the stress is \(76{,}93\) MPa and the exact one \(72{,}72\) MPa. The values are wrong, the sum is right. That this is no accident of this mesh is what the lemma says, and for its proof we draw the upper part of the figure too. Above the nodes \(r_0\), \(r_1\), \(r_2\) are the hat functions \(\psi_0\), \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\), each one at its own node and zero at the neighbouring ones. The pressure acts only on the inner edge, so in the system of equations the force \(p_{\mathrm{a}}\,a\) is at the node \(r_0\) only. At every point between two nodes one function falls from \(1\) towards \(0\) and its neighbour rises at the same rate, so their sum is \(1\) everywhere.

Lemma 17.47 Half-tube equilibrium for the finite element solution (ravnovesje polovice cevi pri rešitvi iz mreže)

Let \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) be the solution of the radial problem of the tube \(a \le r \le b\) of lemma 17.17 on a mesh \(a = r_0 < r_1 < \dots < r_{\mathrm{n}} = b\) with hat functions \(\psi_0, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) (definition 6.25), all nodes free, pressure \(p_{\mathrm{a}}\) at \(r = a\) and a free outer surface. Let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr},\mathrm{g}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}\) be the stresses from \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) by Hooke's law of plane strain at the Gauss point \(g\), and \(w_{\mathrm{g}} = h_{\mathrm{e}}/2\) the weight of the two-point Gauss rule (definition 7.24) in the element \(e\) of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\). Let the system matrix be computed with the same rule, as in the computation of example 17.46. Then for every mesh

\[\sum_{\mathrm{g}} w_{\mathrm{g}}\,\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}} = p_{\mathrm{a}}\,a , \tag{17.45}\]

the sum running over all Gauss points of all elements.

Proof

We show that the sum of the rows of the system of equations for \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) gives exactly equation (17.45).

  1. The system is \(K\,\vek d = \vek f\) with \(f_0 = p_{\mathrm{a}} a\) and \(f_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for \(i \ge 1\) (lemma 17.17: the work of the pressure on a virtual displacement \(v\) is \(p_{\mathrm{a}} a\,v(a)\), and the hat function \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) is one only at node \(i\)).
