By hypothesis the matrix is a sum over Gauss points, \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{g}} w_{\mathrm{g}}\,r_{\mathrm{g}}\,\big(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'(r_{\mathrm{g}})\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}[\psi_{\mathrm{j}}] + \psi_{\mathrm{i}}(r_{\mathrm{g}})\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}[\psi_{\mathrm{j}}]/r_{\mathrm{g}}\big)\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}[\psi_{\mathrm{j}}]\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}[\psi_{\mathrm{j}}]\) are the stresses of the field \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\). By linearity, \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} K_{\mathrm{ij}} d_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{g}} w_{\mathrm{g}}\,r_{\mathrm{g}}\,\big(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr},\mathrm{g}} + \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}/r_{\mathrm{g}}\big)\).
  2. On every element only two hat functions are nonzero, both linear with sum \(1\) (definition 6.25), so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}=0}^{n}\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) on the whole interval and \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \psi_{\mathrm{i}}' = 0\).
  3. We add the equations for \(i = 0, \dots, n\). By step 2 the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr},\mathrm{g}}\) is zero, the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}/r_{\mathrm{g}}\) is \(\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}/r_{\mathrm{g}}\), and the factor \(r_{\mathrm{g}}\) cancels. The left side is \(\sum_{\mathrm{g}} w_{\mathrm{g}}\,\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}\), the sum of the column areas.
  4. The right side of the sum is \(f_0 = p_{\mathrm{a}} a\), because all the other \(f_{\mathrm{i}}\) are zero. Equating gives equation (17.45). \(\square\)

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The check follows the sum of reactions: COOK §10.15 (PDF p. 381).

The lemma says more than it seems. The sum is the Gauss sum for \(\int\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r\), so the mesh satisfies the same half-tube equilibrium as the exact field. If the matrix is integrated exactly, the same proof with integrals in place of sums gives \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = p_{\mathrm{a}}\,a\) for the stress from \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\). The proof uses only that the constant \(1\) lies in the space of hat functions (step 2), just as for the truss, where the reactions balance the load because a rigid displacement lies in the space. The check therefore depends on the space and not on the quality of the mesh. The hypothesis that all nodes are free enters where the rows are added: if the displacement of a node were prescribed, its row would gain a reaction, and the reaction would appear in the sum, as for the truss. We test it on three mistakes, each introduced into the computation of example 17.46.

  • A coarse mesh \(n = 1\). The sum is \(1{,}2\) MN/m \(= p\,a\) up to round-off, although the hoop stress at the bore is \(88{,}45\) MPa instead of \(78{,}00\), an error of \(+13{,}4\,\%\) (example 17.46). We saw the same at \(n = 2\): the columns deviate from the exact curve, their sum does not. The check does not find the discretization error and cannot, because it holds on every mesh. It is found by comparison with the Lamé solution or by refining the mesh (check (f) of section 7.10.3, figure 17.73).
  • A wrong pressure in the data, \(p = 3\) MPa instead of \(30\) MPa. The sum is \(0{,}12\) MN/m, which is \(p\,a\) with the entered pressure, and it agrees with itself. If we compare it with \(p\,a\) at the pressure the task demands, the error is \(-90\,\%\). The check finds the mistake only when the computer has the true datum from the task, not from the input. Refining the mesh does not find this mistake, because the relative errors at \(p = 3\) MPa are the same as at \(30\) MPa (the computation is linear in \(p\)).
  • A wrong modulus, \(E = 19{,}6\) GPa instead of \(196\) GPa. The sum and all the stresses are unchanged (\(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a) = 79{,}218\) MPa in both cases, because \(E\) does not enter the stresses of this force problem), but the displacement is \(168{,}71\ \mu\)m instead of \(16{,}87\ \mu\)m. Only comparing the displacement with an approximate or exact calculation (check (d)) or a review of units and data (check (g)) finds it. The stress check is blind to this mistake.

The list does not say that the real model is now verified. It says only which step catches which mistake. Section 7.10.3 did the same for the truss, and COOK lists mistakes that a program does not detect by itself: elements of the wrong type, a coarse mesh, supports wrong in position, kind or direction, a misplaced decimal point, and an element defined twice that we do not see on a plot of the mesh (COOK §10.13, PDF pp. 377-378). A program checks element distortion and unconnected nodes, but it cannot know whether the problem we wanted is the one defined, whether the material data are right, or whether the supports are in the right places (COOK §10.14, PDF p. 380). Since the program does not know this, the analyst must keep a record of the sources of data, assumptions, tests and the version of the program, so that after an interruption the work can be resumed or reviewed by someone else (COOK §10.13, PDF pp. 378-379).

17.9.4 Critique of the result and the decision

The sixth step is the critique. First the question whether the result looks strange, and then the quantities we already know (COOK §10.15, PDF pp. 380-381). COOK warns that stresses computed from displacements are less accurate than the displacements, so we do not trust them if the displacements are doubtful (COOK §10.15, PDF p. 382).

In our tube the displacements are trustworthy but the stresses do not reach the boundary condition. Let us draw the radial stress in the first four elements at the bore at \(n = 16\) (axes: radius in mm, stress in MPa). The blackwhite curve is the exact stress, which starts at the bore at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -p = -30\) MPa, as the boundary condition demands (theorem 11.28, step 7 of its proof). The blue segments are the stress from the mesh, one in each element. In an element the derivative \(u_{\mathrm{h}}'\) is constant while the exact derivative changes along it, so the segment meets the curve in the middle of the element (lemma 17.19) and moves away from it towards both ends. At the bore the first element gives \(-27{,}12\) MPa, which is \(2{,}88\) MPa or \(9{,}59\,\%\) too little, and \(-28{,}54\) MPa at \(n = 32\), \(4{,}86\,\%\) too little. This deviation is an estimate of the error that needs no exact solution, because we know the condition from the task. The hoop stress is wrong by \(1{,}56\,\%\) and \(0{,}80\,\%\) at these two meshes, so the deviation of the boundary condition is six times larger than the error it estimates (\(6{,}15\) and \(6{,}11\)). The factor six is an observation on this tube, not a law: it says that the estimate is here on the safe side, and on another task it would have to be measured again.

If the critique finds a mistake, the dashed arrow sends the analysis back to the model and the mesh. The seventh step is the decision. The mesh with \(n = 16\) is within the \(2\,\%\) tolerance (\(1{,}43\,\%\)), but the error is one-sided and the deviation at the boundary says that the stress at the bore has not yet settled. So we use theorem 17.14. In the right part of figure 17.75 we draw the values \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}(a)\) against the element size \(h\) (axes): the points for \(n = 4, 8, 16, 32\) lie almost on a straight line, which means an order close to \(1\). The two triples of meshes gave \(0{,}93\) and \(0{,}96\), so we take \(q = 1\). The extrapolation is then the line through the last two points, extended to \(h = 0\): from \(n = 16\) to \(32\) the size \(h\) is halved and the value rises from \(92{,}68\) to \(93{,}34\) MPa, that is by \(0{,}66\) MPa, and one more such half is left to \(h = 0\). We get \(2 \cdot 93{,}3449 - 92{,}6803 = 94{,}01\) MPa. The exact value is \(94{,}02\) MPa, an error of \(-0{,}013\,\%\), and \(p_{\mathrm{Y}} = 30 \cdot 220/94{,}01 = 70{,}21\) MPa. Had we taken the wrong \(q = 2\), which is right for the displacement, we would get \((4 \cdot 93{,}34 - 92{,}68)/3 = 93{,}57\) MPa, an error of \(-0{,}48\,\%\): within the tolerance, but more than thirty times larger than with the observed order (section 17.3).

The decision has a remainder that computing does not reduce. The discretization error at \(n = 16\) is \(1{,}43\,\%\), the difference between plane strain and closed ends is \(0{,}53\,\%\) and the difference between open and closed ends is \(3{,}2\,\%\). So we first decide what ends the tube really has (modelling error). Only then does it make sense to refine the mesh, since at \(1{,}43\,\%\) plane strain and closed ends (\(0{,}53\,\%\)) are not yet distinguished. For open ends \(p_{\mathrm{Y}} = 68{,}35\) MPa, the lowest of the three, and whoever does not know the ends designs by it.

17.9.5 Verification and validation

What the tables of example 17.46 do not cover is the question whether the model is the right one at all. Let us draw the three things every analysis has.

At the top is the physical system, the real tube with oil. From it, by idealizations, we make the mathematical model: the equations, the two boundary conditions and the data \(E\) and \(\nu\). With a mesh we turn it into the computational model with the solution \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\). Two questions can be asked. The blue arrow compares the computational model with the mathematical one: did we solve the equations right. The orange dashed arrow compares the computation with the real system: did we solve the right equations. ONATE1 has two terms for these comparisons and keeps them apart.

Definition 17.48 Verification and validation of a computational model (preverjanje in potrjevanje računskega modela)

Let a physical system be given, its mathematical model (equations and data) and a computational model (the solution of that model by finite elements). Verification is the process of determining that the computational model accurately represents the mathematical model and its solution, whether or not the model corresponds to reality. It has two parts:

  1. code verification: we gain confidence that the program solves the equations of the model correctly. It is done by comparison with simple cases that have an exact solution.
  2. calculation verification: for this computational case we estimate the discretization error, by refining the mesh or by raising the order of the elements.

Validation is the assessment whether the mathematical and the computational model represent the physical system for the intended purpose: by comparison with measurements on a model or on a real structure. A large deviation for an already verified program means that the chosen model is not suitable.

Source: ONATE1 §1.4.4 (PDF pp. 31-33): verification shows that we solve the problems accurately, validation that we solve the right problem.

The names say what they establish. To verify means in everyday use to look whether something holds, and verification here looks whether the solution holds for the model we wrote down. To validate means to establish by a measurement or a witness that something is so, and validation here compares the model with a measurement on the real system. For the tube, the first part, code verification, is the comparison of \(u(a)\) and the stresses with the Lamé solution (theorem 11.28): the exact solution of the mathematical model is the yardstick (the table in example 17.46, displacement \(0{,}004\,\%\) at \(n = 32\)). The second part, calculation verification, is the estimate from this section: from three meshes with Richardson's extrapolation and from the deviation of the boundary condition. For a tube with a groove, for which no exact solution exists, this would be the only part of verification we have for the computation itself, while the program would still be verified on the tube without the groove. ONATE1 also mentions manufactured solutions: we choose an arbitrary displacement field, compute from the equations the load that produces it, and check whether the program finds the field (ONATE1 §1.4.4, PDF pp. 33-35). Here we only name this way.

We have no validation for our tube, which is why a question mark stands at the orange arrow. The book has no measured strains on a real tube, so the answer \(p_{\mathrm{Y}} = 70{,}2\) MPa (plane strain) holds for the model: a homogeneous isotropic linearly elastic material, the yield stress \(220\) MPa and the von Mises condition. It is verified and not validated. Among the unvalidated idealizations are these three: the material is homogeneous, yielding is described by the von Mises stress, and the ends of the tube are fixed as one of the three possibilities.

17.9.6 Software

The plan needs a tool, a program. Programs are not written by the average analyst but by researchers, students and companies, their development is expensive, and users stay loyal to the program they already know. For this reason COOK does not compare products, which change quickly, and neither do we name any. The documentation is part of the system we test, and it must be read when choosing a program (COOK, PDF p. 384). Code verification of definition 17.48 applies to a program we buy just as to one we write: the tube with the Lamé solution is a test that can be run on every program in which a pressure on the inner edge can be prescribed.

17.9.7 Plate with a hole: a plan without numbers

Chapter 11 left the question how large the stress at a hole in a finite plate is, and wrote it as the yardstick for a numerical result: Kirsch's factor \(3\) (theorem 11.57). The plate is \(200 \times 200\) mm with a hole of radius \(a = 10\) mm and a tensile load \(\sigma_0 = 50\) MPa, the largest stress is \(3\sigma_0 = 150\) MPa, first yielding is at \(\sigma_0 = 73{,}33\) MPa, and the error of the load at the edge due to the finite width is \(2{,}5\,\%\) (section 11.13.6). Let us see what the plan would demand for a finite element computation, and what we can already say from the book without a single mesh result.

Plane elements are in chapter 15, but the book does not carry out the computation of this plate with them, so there are no mesh numbers here. What we can compute is a yardstick for the mesh. Figure 17.77 shows how the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) along the \(y\) axis falls from the edge of the hole (equation (11.90)). First the axes: horizontally the distance from the centre of the hole in radii \(r/a\), vertically \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\sigma_0\). The curve starts at the peak at \(3\) and falls to \(1{,}93\) at \(r = 1{,}25\,a\), \(1{,}52\) at \(1{,}5\,a\), \(1{,}22\) at \(2\,a\) and \(1{,}07\) at \(3\,a\), towards the value \(1\) far from the hole. So the stress changes over a length of the size of the hole radius, and from here follows how fine the mesh must be.

An element in which the stress is constant cannot give the peak. The mean of a function over an interval is smaller than its largest value when the function is smaller than it everywhere except at one end, and the curve of the figure has its peak at \(r = a\). The orange segment shows an element of size \(h = a\) at the hole: the mean of the exact stress over it is \(1{,}6875\,\sigma_0\) (SymPy, outlines/ch-modeliranje/num-09.out), \(56\,\%\) of the peak. The blue segment at \(h = a/4\) gives \(2{,}376\,\sigma_0\), \(79\,\%\), and at \(h = a/8\) still only \(2{,}635\,\sigma_0\), \(88\,\%\). For small \(h\) the mean is about \(3\,\sigma_0 - 3{,}5\,\sigma_0\,h/a\): half the slope of the curve at the peak (\(-7\,\sigma_0/a\)), because the mean over an interval of length \(h\) is about the value at its middle. At \(h = a/8\) this approximation gives \(2{,}56\,\sigma_0\) instead of \(2{,}635\,\sigma_0\). The shortfall is therefore proportional to \(h/a\), and for \(2\,\%\) of the peak (\(0{,}06\,\sigma_0\)) a constant stress in the element would need \(h\) of about \(a/58\) (the exact mean gives \(a/57\), SymPy). This is why the plan for the plate uses higher-order elements or stress recovery (section 17.4), and refines the mesh towards the hole and not everywhere. The conclusion holds for elements with constant stress and does not say how much error the elements of chapter 15 would have.

The remaining steps of the plan follow the tube: a plane stress model of a quarter of the plate with mirror conditions on the axis planes (the idea of lemma 7.39, in general chapter 19), the question (the largest stress at a point at the hole, hence a mesh as fine as for stresses, section 17.9.2), the hand calculation (Kirsch's factor \(3\), the correction for the finite width is not computed, section 11.13.6), the check (the resultant of the forces on the edge \(x = \pm 100\) mm is \(\sigma_0 \cdot 200\ \text{mm} \cdot t\), like the reactions of the truss), the sequence of meshes and theorem 17.14, and the critique (the deviation of the value at the edge of the hole from the free-edge condition, as for the tube). Whoever gets a value near \(150\) MPa from the computation must not conclude that the mesh error is small: the difference from Kirsch's value also contains the effect of the finite width, which the book estimates only for the load on the edge (\(2{,}5\,\%\)), not for the stress at the hole. So we judge the mesh from three meshes and not from the comparison with \(3\sigma_0\).

17.9.8 What we have shown

The plan of an analysis is seven steps: question and tolerance, hand calculation, model, sequence of meshes, check, critique, decision (figure 17.72). On the tube we showed what each gives. The hand calculation hit the order of magnitude (\(60\) and \(75\) against \(78\) MPa), not \(2\,\%\) (with equation (17.44) and the Lamé field). The displacement and the stress converge at different speeds, \(0{,}017\,\%\) and \(1{,}43\,\%\) at \(n = 16\) (comparison of the columns of the table, figure 17.73). The check of the half-tube equilibrium holds on every mesh (lemma 17.47, proof with hat functions) and therefore does not find a coarse mesh, but it does find a wrong pressure if we compare it with the task (computed cases). The deviation of the boundary condition is six times larger than the error of the hoop stress (a computed case, not a law). Extrapolation with the observed order \(1\) gives \(94{,}01\) MPa against the exact \(94{,}02\) MPa. Larger than the error of \(1{,}43\,\%\) is the difference between open and closed ends, \(3{,}2\,\%\), and the mesh does not reduce it. The model is verified, not validated.

For the plate with a hole the plan is written without mesh numbers, because the book does not carry out the computation of this plate with the plane elements of chapter 15. The yardstick for the mesh, the mean of the exact stress over an element at the hole (\(56\,\%\) of the peak at \(h = a\)), is computed from Kirsch's solution.

17.10 Connections

The course abbreviations are the same as in section 1.19. Each section of this chapter treats one or two of the three errors that definition 17.2 in section 17.1 separates: the modelling error, the discretization error and the numerical error. In figure 17.8 these are three steps on the axis of the wanted quantity, from the physical system to the number from the program. For each section we say where its result returns, and for each connection also which of the three steps it shortens and which ones it leaves.

  • Hierarchy of models and the modelling error (section 17.1): lemma 17.3 says that the ratio of the shear part to the bending part of the tip deflection of a cantilever is \(E/(4kG)\,(H/L)^2\). For a steel cantilever with a rectangular section the Euler-Bernoulli model is below the Timoshenko model by \(16{,}32\) % at \(L/H = 2\), the first dot of the blue curve. That is the share of the shear piece \(0{,}796\ \mu\)m in the tip deflection, the piece that the assumption of a plane section without a shear angle leaves out. At \(L/H = 20\) the difference is only \(0{,}19\) %, the last dot of the same curve, because the shear piece grows with \(L\) and the bending piece with \(L^3\). The same question, when a one-dimensional model still suffices, returns for surface models in plates (MK, AK, chapter 18) and shells (MK, AK, chapter 22), and for flexible robot links, where the beam is the model of the link (DSK, chapter 28). This is the modelling error, and the mesh does not reduce it: a single Euler-Bernoulli beam element already gives the deflection of that model exactly (three points on the lower axis coincide), while the whole gap to the plane model stays.
  • Body to model, point force and submodel (section 17.2): theorem 17.9 proves that the total potential energy of a point force on a plane body is not bounded below. The reason is in figure 17.20: a field that equals \(1\) under the force and narrows around it has less and less energy, while the work of the force on it stays the same. So by corollary 17.10 the displacement under the force grows without bound on nested meshes (in the ring model every doubling adds about \(\ln 2\) in the unit \(F/(2\pi T)\)), while in a bar or a beam it does not (chapters 7 and 12). The load on a small area, which the point force replaces, is treated in chapter 25 (DSK). The submodel of lemma 17.5, loaded on the cut by the displacement of the full model, rests on the uniqueness of the boundary value problem (theorem 11.4) and on Saint-Venant's principle of section 11.11. The half model of lemma 7.39 is extended by chapter 19 to mirror planes in several dimensions and to constraints between nodes (AK). The point force, the submodel and the half model are decisions about the modelling error, which a finer mesh does not correct.
  • Mesh convergence (section 17.3): the order of convergence from three nested meshes and Richardson's theorem 17.14 give for the first eigenvalue of a bar with both ends fixed, on three successive triples of meshes, the orders \(2{,}05\), \(2{,}02\) and \(2{,}01\). The first is \(\log_2(d_1/d_2) = \log_2(1{,}613/0{,}390)\), the binary logarithm of the ratio of the two distances between the points of three meshes. The extrapolation steps on from the value of the finer mesh by a third of the difference \(d_1\): at order \(2\) the error of the finer mesh is a quarter of the error of the coarse one, so the difference between the meshes is three times the error that still remains. The meshes with \(n = 4\) and \(8\) elements give \(9{,}867227\), \(0{,}0024\) below \(\pi^2\), and the meshes with \(n = 16\) and \(32\) a value that differs from \(\pi^2\) by only \(10^{-5}\). The same procedure holds for every quantity computed on a sequence of meshes, so also for temperatures (VT, AK, chapter 14) and for displacements of plane elements (AK, chapter 15). The discretization error falls as the mesh is refined, the modelling error and the numerical error stay.
  • Stresses from FE results (section 17.4): corollary 17.18 states the error estimate for finite elements promised by chapter 1 (the mean value theorem), and the stresses are one order worse than the displacements, because we compute them from the derivative of the displacement: in figure 17.73 the error of the displacement falls to a quarter at every doubling of the elements, the error of the stress only to a half. The equivalent stress of definition 2.107 and the largest shear stress of theorem 2.93 are computed at the inner edge of the tube of chapter 11 from element stresses, which satisfy the boundary condition only in the limit (the circles at the edge: with four elements \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -19{,}32\) instead of \(-30\) MPa). For continuum elements (AK, chapter 15) the Gauss points are the stress points, which is the same idea as the exact strain at one point of an element (the dots in the middles of the elements lie almost on the Lamé curves). A finer mesh reduces only the discretization error of the stresses, the modelling error and the numerical error stay.
  • Mesh quality (section 17.5): lemma 17.22 proves that the bar element with three nodes, its middle node at the fraction \(c\) of the length, has \(J > 0\) on the whole element exactly for \(1/4 < c < 3/4\), the grey band in figure 17.39. Outside the band the map folds over and two values of \(\xi\) mean the same point of the bar. The letter \(J\) here is the one-dimensional \(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}\xi\), in chapter 2 it is \(J = \det\mat F\), the ratio of volumes (lemma 2.77), and \(J_2\) is the second invariant of the deviator (equation (2.105)). For plane and solid elements the quality measures are only named, their Jacobian belongs to chapter 15 (AK). The quarter-point element (\(c = 1/4\), on the edge of the band) captures a smooth field worse than the element with its middle node at the midpoint, and a field that behaves like \(\sqrt{x}\) exactly. The shape and the arrangement of elements change only the discretization error, they do not reduce the modelling error.
  • Large systems of equations (section 17.6): lemma 17.29 gives the condition number \(\kappa\) of definition 6.31 for a bar fixed at one end and free at the other, \(175{,}1\), \(16\,370\) and \(1\,622\,757\) for \(10\), \(100\) and \(1000\) elements. Ten times more elements raise it almost a hundredfold (slope \(2\)), because the softest shape is cut into more and shorter steps and its eigenvalue falls like \(1/n^2\), while the largest one stays below \(4\). The band of the matrix from lemma 7.42 and one factorization for several load cases from lemma 7.47 remain valid for large models too. Constraints that chapter 19 eliminates from the system reduce the number of unknowns, while the penalty method keeps them and, by lemma 12.29, worsens \(\kappa\). The reduced model of chapter 21 shrinks the system to a few modes (DSK). The locking of continuum elements for a nearly incompressible material is a penalty system like the shear locking of the beam (AK, chapter 15). The section treats the numerical error: a finer mesh reduces the discretization error but raises \(\kappa\) and with it the upper bound of the numerical error: with \(1000\) elements about six of the sixteen digits are lost.
  • Nonlinear statics (section 17.7): Newton's method, which converges quadratically when the tangent stiffness at the root is not zero, and theorem 17.35, by which a column made of a rigid bar with an imperfection and a horizontal spring has a limit load of \(0{,}931\) of the critical one at \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\), complete the linear buckling analysis of definition 12.51 and the upper bound of theorem 12.53. The linear analysis gives the same critical load for both column models and cannot tell the stable model from the unstable one. Theorems 13.96 and 8.148 are about the perfect column, imperfections require a nonlinear model. The modelling error here is the linear model, which does not know the limit load: its straight line passes the top and goes on upwards, while the true path turns down beyond the top. At \(p = 0{,}9\) the linear model gives the rotation \(0{,}0090\) rad instead of \(0{,}0955\) rad. The numerical error is the stopped iteration, and a model with one degree of freedom has no discretization error. Plasticity and nonlinear contact are not treated in the book.
  • Nonlinear dynamics (section 17.8): the Newmark family of definition 17.36 contains the trapezoidal rule of chapter 10 (theorem 10.95) and central differences (theorem 10.99). Stability for one mode follows definition 10.94. For \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) and \(\beta = 0{,}3025\) the spectral radius on the vertical line \(\omega\Delta t = 2\pi/20\) is \(0{,}995\), a little below \(1\). After twenty steps, that is after one period, the amplitude is \(0{,}99520^{20} = 0{,}9082\) of the initial one, which means that numerical damping damps the low modes too. Physical damping with a damping matrix (DSK, chapter 20) is a different notion and must not be confused with the damping of a scheme. For the pendulum of theorem 8.139, released from the horizontal position, the trapezoidal rule with the step \(2\pi/20\) (in units of \(\sqrt{l/g}\)) lengthens the period by \(0{,}57\) %: the dots of the scheme lag behind the accurate curve (the figure shows the twice longer step \(2\pi/10\) with a lag of \(2{,}23\) %, so that it is visible). Unlike for a linear system it does not conserve the energy exactly (theorem 17.44): in three swings it deviates by at most \(8{,}06 \cdot 10^{-3}\) from the initial value \(1\). The step limit through the ratio \(h/c\) of chapter 13 holds for explicit steps. A smaller step reduces the discretization error in time, a more accurate Newton iteration the numerical error, and the modelling error (a point mass on a rigid rod, without friction and air) stays.
  • Plan of an analysis (section 17.9): the steps and checks of sections 7.10.1 and 7.10.3 and the split of errors of section 7.10.4 are the procedure, and section 17.9 applies it to the tube of theorem 11.28: the discretization error of the von Mises stress at the bore at 16 elements (\(1{,}43\) % on the blue line) is larger than the difference between plane strain and closed ends (the dashed line at \(0{,}53\) %), while the difference between open and closed ends (\(3{,}2\) %, \(96{,}56\) against \(93{,}53\) MPa) is a modelling error that the mesh does not reduce, because the axial stress of the ends enters neither of the stresses that the mesh computes. Chapter 29 repeats the analysis in a loop, so there it matters which error each step reduces.
  • Planned in other chapters: plane and solid elements with the isoparametric map and the Jacobian matrix in chapter 15, symmetry and constraints in chapter 19, damping matrices in chapter 20, reduction and the eigenproblem of large systems in chapter 21, contact and Flamant's solution in chapter 25. Plasticity, large strains, the arc-length method, iterative solvers and mesh generation algorithms are only named.
  • Limits of the chapter: the error expansion \(e = C h^q + \dots\) for a general FE quantity, the number of lost digits of about \(\log_{10}\kappa\), the quality limits of plane and solid elements, the ZZ error estimate and adaptive meshing are cited from sources, not proved. Newmark stability is proved for a linear system mode by mode and only on the line \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\), not for the general region \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\) and not for a nonlinear system. In figure 17.61 the proved part is thus one curve, and the rest of the region is cited from COOK (11.13-7).
